Certified bounds on optimization problems in quantum theory

Younes Naceur Email: Younes.Naceur@icfo.eu Affiliation: ICFO - Institut de Ciencies Fotoniques, The Barcelona Institute of Science and Technology, Av. Carl Friedrich Gauss 3, 08860 Castelldefels (Barcelona), Spain Affiliation: LAAS-CNRS - Laboratoire d’Analyse et d’Architecture des Systèmes, Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique, Toulouse, France    Jie Wang Affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Mathematical Sciences, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China    Victor Magron Affiliation: LAAS-CNRS - Laboratoire d’Analyse et d’Architecture des Systèmes, Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique, Toulouse, France Affiliation: Institute of Mathematics, Toulouse, France    Antonio Acín Affiliation: ICFO - Institut de Ciencies Fotoniques, The Barcelona Institute of Science and Technology, Av. Abstract

Semidefinite relaxations of polynomial optimization have become a central tool for addressing the non-convex optimization problems over non-commutative operators that are ubiquitous in quantum information theory and, more in general, quantum physics. Yet, as these global relaxation methods are solved numerically, the bounds issued by the semidefinite solver can - and often do - exceed the global optimum, undermining their certifiability. To counter this issue, we introduce a framework for extracting rigorous certified bounds on non-commutative optimization problems from inexact numerical data, and apply it to several paradigmatic problems in quantum information theory. An extension to sparsity and symmetry-adapted semidefinite relaxations is also provided and compared to the general dense scheme. Our results establish rational post-processing as a practical route to reliable certification, pushing semidefinite optimization toward a certifiable standard for quantum information science.

keywords
Quantum Information, Polynomial Optimization, Semidefinite Programming, Computer-assisted proof

1 Introduction

Non-commutative polynomial optimization (NPO) investigates the task of bounding the spectrum of a polynomial in non-commuting operator-valued variables, where said underlying operators are subject to polynomial inequality and equality constraints. As this matches the natural setting of optimization problems in quantum theory, many applications of NPO have been studied therein. Such problem classes comprise, not exclusively, the computation of the maximal quantum violation of a given Bell expression [42], the ground-state problem of many-body quantum systems [55], as well as fundamental problems in causality [3], and contextuality [52]. Generically, polynomial optimization problems (in commuting or non-commuting variables) are hard to solve exactly, which is why often relaxations of these problems are the only tools available. By virtue of relaxations, optimization is performed over a bigger, often convex feasible set. Note that relaxation to a convex problem is often crucial for its computational tractability, since for these problems a manifold of efficient numerical methods exist. Moreover, they are free from local optima, yielding rigorous lower and upper bounds to minimization and maximization problems, respectively.

The Navascués-Pironio-Acín (NPA) hierarchy [43, 49] constitutes a very general relaxation framework based on available convex computational methods that allows one to obtain a monotone series of outer bounds {λd}d=dmin∞\{\lambda_{d}\}_{d=d_{\min}}^{\infty} (upper bounds to maximization problems) for a given NPO. The bounds are obtained numerically by solving a series of Semidefinite Programs (SDP) of increasing sizes, where under mild conditions this series converges to the global optimum of the problem, λ∞=λmax\lambda_{\infty}=\lambda_{\max}.

This hierarchy has been extensively studied and applied to several emblematic problems in quantum theory. In recent years, several efforts have been made to extend the efficiency, scalability, and applicability of non-commutative semidefinite relaxations. As in the commuting case, the exploitation of the problem’s sparsity structure has been shown to significantly improve the scalability of the hierarchy [27, 54]. To complement sparsity exploitation, one can further reduce the size of the underlying optimization problem by exploiting the physical symmetries of the underlying problems [51]. To obtain tighter bounds at a given relaxation order, the use of first-order optimality conditions [19, 5] has been explored. Various extensions of the hierarchy, increasing its applicability, include the trace optimization of non-commutative polynomials [11], as well as optimization over polynomials in state expectation values [28]. Recently, the framework was also extended to deal with NPO’s subject to differential constraints [4].

While the computational efficiency of semidefinite relaxations is one of their principal advantages, it also entails a significant limitation. In practice, the underlying semidefinite programs are solved using floating-point arithmetic, and the resulting feasible points satisfy the positivity and equality constraints of the problem only approximately. Consequently, the outer bounds obtained from hierarchies such as NPA, which are often described in the literature as certifying that a given objective value cannot exceed the numerical bound λd\lambda_{d}, do not constitute formal certificates. As will be illustrated in later sections, the unavoidable rounding errors inherent to numerical solvers can invalidate the positivity or feasibility of the solution. This absence of numerical exactness constitutes an unresolved bottleneck for using semidefinite relaxations as proof systems in quantum theory.

Although obtaining exact, rather than approximate, bounds is an evident step toward mathematical rigor, there are additional, more practical arguments for their necessity: Many optimization protocols, —such as branch-and-bound [6], or constraint-generation schemes [20] — rely on iterative schemes, reusing previously computed SDP bounds as input for subsequent computations. These methods typically rely on the exactness of the input bounds; however, if the input bounds are only approximate, the inference chains often lose validity, undermining their claimed guaranties. Similarly, in witness-based scenarios, such as randomness certification or entanglement detection, a numerical upper bound that is even slightly too low can lead to wrong physical conclusions. Establishing exact, algebraically verifiable SDP bounds is therefore a prerequisite for turning semidefinite relaxations into rigorous tools for certification in quantum information science, bridging the gap between efficient numerical computation and mathematical proof.

To address this issue, we present a three-step post-processing procedure that turns numerical SDP outputs into rigorous, exact certificates for non-commutative polynomial optimization. The method applies to constrained and unconstrained problems, and is extended to sparsity- and symmetry-adapted scenarios. Starting from a numerical Gram-matrix certificate, we (1) round the floating-point solution to nearby rational data, (2) project it (Frobenius-optimally) onto the affine subspace enforcing the certificate equalities, and (3) lift the resulting matrix back into the positive-semidefinite (PSD) cone to restore feasibility. After the rounding step, the subsequent algebraic operations are performed using exact rational arithmetic, thereby avoiding any further round-off error. Additionally, when the projected matrix lies strictly inside the PSD cone, our method can be used to further tighten the numerical bound.

The manuscript is organized as follows: Section 2 introduces the theory of semidefinite relaxations for non-commutative polynomial optimization problems. In Section 3 we present our algorithmic contribution, that is a rigorous method of how to obtain certifiable bounds from numerically inaccurate certificates. Section 4 extends the certification scheme to the sparsity- and symmetry-adapted version of the hierarchy. Sections 5 and 6 are dedicated to our numerical tests. In Section 5, we apply our method to the maximal violation of a family of bipartite Bell inequalities, as well as a variant of the tilted CHSH inequality, and investigate its performance. Section 6 deals with the application of our scheme to certify bounds on quantum many-body ground-state observables. In Section 7 we conclude our work and outline directions for further research.

2 Semidefinite relaxations for non-commutative optimization problems

We start by presenting the polynomial optimization problems analyzed in this work. Given a separable Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H}, let ℬ⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}) be the set of bounded operators acting on ℋ\mathcal{H}. We consider the problem of finding the maximal eigenvalue λmax\lambda_{\max} of a polynomial f⁡(X¯)f(\underline{X}) with rational coefficients in tuples of bounded, self-adjoint operator-valued variables X¯={X1,…,Xn}\underline{X}=\{X_{1},...,X_{n}\} over a feasible set KK given by

{X¯⊂ℬ(ℋ)|hi(X¯)=0,gi(X¯)⪰0;hi∈H,gi∈G},\small\{\underline{X}\subset\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})\,|\,h_{i}(\underline{X})=0,g_{i}(\underline{X})\succeq 0;\,h_{i}\in H,\,g_{i}\in G\}, (1)

which is characterized by a set of polynomial inequality and equality constraints G={gi​(X¯)}i=1,..,mGG=\{g_{i}(\underline{X})\}_{i=1,..,m_{G}} and H={hi​(X¯)}i=1,..,mHH=\{h_{i}(\underline{X})\}_{i=1,..,m_{H}}, respectively. The dimension of the variables X¯\underline{X} is unrestricted, allowing for feasible solutions acting on a Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} of arbitrary dimension — a key feature of this framework, enabling the treatment of device-independent scenarios in quantum information science.

Without loss of generality, only maximization problems are considered in this section. The generic optimization problem then reads as

sup|ψ⟩,ℋ,X¯⊂ℬ⁡(ℋ)⟨ψ|​f​(X¯)​|ψ⟩\displaystyle\sup_{\ket{\psi},\mathcal{H},\underline{X}\subset\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})}\qquad\bra{\psi}f(\underline{X})\ket{\psi} (2)
s.t.hi​(X¯)=0,i=1,…,mH,\displaystyle\qquad\mathrm{s.t.}\qquad\quad\quad\,\,h_{i}(\underline{X})=0,\qquad i=1,...,m_{H},
gi(X¯)⪰0,i=1,…,mG.\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\,\,\,\,\,g_{i}(\underline{X})\succeq 0,\qquad i=1,...,m_{G}.

The optimization can be interpreted as follows: We maximize over all possible (finite and infinite dimensional) Hilbert spaces ℋ\mathcal{H}, the normalized states therein, |ψ⟩∈ℋ\ket{\psi}\in\mathcal{H}, as well as the tuples of bounded operators X¯⊂ℬ⁡(ℋ)\underline{X}\subset\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}) acting upon it. This is equivalent to optimizing for the maximal eigenvalue of the polynomial f⁡(X¯)f(\underline{X}) s.t. X¯∈K\underline{X}\in K. Generically, this problem is non-convex and computationally intractable [30], which is why studying a relaxed form of the problem is often necessary.

2.1 Relaxations of polynomial optimization

One starts by recasting the optimization as a problem of non-negativity

infλ∈ℝλ\displaystyle\inf_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}}\qquad\qquad\lambda (3)
s.t.λ​1−f⁡(X¯)⪰0∀X¯∈K\displaystyle\mathrm{s.t.}\qquad\lambda{1}-f(\underline{X})\succeq 0\quad\forall\underline{X}\in K

which is equivalent to (2) so far: one rephrases the maximization problem (2) as a minimization problem over valid upper bounds, where the optima of the two problems coincide. Above, we denoted the identity operator by 1{1}. In what follows, by a slight abuse of notation, the same symbol will also be used to denote the constant polynomial 1 and the identity matrix. Now, as the task of characterizing the set of non-negative polynomials 𝒫K​⟨X¯⟩\mathcal{P}_{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle on a basic closed semialgebraic set KK is again a computationally intractable task, a version of a central result by Helton and McCullough [22] is used. To do so, we rephrase Problem (3) in the framework of operator theory.

Let 𝕂∈{ℝ,ℂ}\mathbb{K}\in\{\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}\} denote the underlying field of real or complex numbers, respectively. We then consider all polynomial objects as members of the ∗*-algebra 𝕂​⟨X¯⟩\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle spanned by X¯\underline{X}, and equipped with the involution ∗*, acting on 𝕂​⟨X¯⟩\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle by reversing the word order of monomials and conjugating their coefficients. Given r∈𝕂​⟨X¯⟩r\in\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle, the polynomial r∗​rr^{*}r is called a Hermitian square. Sums of the form ∑iri∗​ri\sum_{i}r_{i}^{*}r_{i} are called Sums-of-Hermitian-Squares (SOHS), and Sums-of-Squares (SOS) when 𝕂=ℝ\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{R}.

In addition, we define the quadratic module 𝒦\mathcal{K} associated to the feasible set KK as

𝒦\displaystyle\mathcal{K} ={p∈𝕂⟨X¯⟩|p=∑iri∗ri+∑i,jui​j∗giui​j+\displaystyle=\{p\in\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle\ |\,p=\sum_{i}r_{i}^{*}r_{i}+\sum_{i,j}u_{ij}^{*}g_{i}u_{ij}+
∑i,jvi​j∗hiwi​j;ri,ui​j,vi​j,wi​j∈𝕂⟨X¯⟩}.\displaystyle\sum_{i,j}v_{ij}^{*}h_{i}w_{ij};\,\,r_{i},u_{ij},v_{ij},w_{ij}\in\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle\}. (4)

A quadratic module is said to fulfill the Archimedean property if and only if there exists some C>0C>0 s.t. C−∑i=1nXi2∈𝒦C-\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}^{2}\in\mathcal{K}. This property guarantees boundedness of the feasible operator tuples, a crucial aspect for the asymptotic convergence of the hierarchy.

Theorem 1 (Helton–McCullough Positivstellensatz [22]).

Let KK be a basic closed semialgebraic set with associated Archimedean quadratic module 𝒦\mathcal{K}. If p∈𝕂​⟨X¯⟩p\in\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle is positive definite on KK, then p∈𝒦p\in\mathcal{K}.

Using this result, we rephrase the non-negativity condition as

infλ∈ℝλ\displaystyle\inf_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}}\qquad\lambda (5)
s.t.λ​1−f∈𝒦,\displaystyle\qquad\,\,\,\,\mathrm{s.t.}\qquad\lambda{1}-f\in\mathcal{K},

where we passed from explicit operator evaluations f⁡(X)f(X) over explicit Hilbert spaces and operator tuples to abstract polynomials ff in an algebra, which is why the optimization variables ℋ\mathcal{H} and X¯\underline{X} are omitted. The next step consists of relaxing this problem by not considering all polynomials in 𝒦\mathcal{K}, but only those up to a certain degree. To do so, we restrict the summands of p∈𝒦p\in\mathcal{K} to have maximal degree 2​d2d, which defines 𝒦2​d\mathcal{K}_{2d}, the truncated quadratic module of degree 2​d2d. This allows one to define the dd-th level of the non-commutative SOHS hierarchy, which is dual to the NPA hierarchy:

λd=infλ∈ℝλ\displaystyle\lambda_{d}=\inf_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}}\qquad\lambda (6)
s.t.λ​1−f∈𝒦2​d,\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\,\,\,\,\mathrm{s.t.}\qquad\lambda{1}-f\in\mathcal{K}_{2d},

dmin=⌈max⁡{deg⁡(f),deg⁡(hi),deg⁡(gi)}/2⌉.d_{\min}=\lceil\max\{\mathrm{deg}(f),\mathrm{deg}(h_{i}),\mathrm{deg}(g_{i})\}/2\rceil. (7)

Now, obviously, 𝒦2​d⊆𝒦2​d+2⊆…⊆𝒫K​⟨X¯⟩\mathcal{K}_{2d}\subseteq\mathcal{K}_{2d+2}\subseteq...\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle, which implies λdmin≥λdmin+1≥⋯≥λmax\lambda_{d_{\min}}\geq\lambda_{d_{\min}+1}\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{\max}, yielding a series of monotonically decreasing upper bounds λd\lambda_{d} to the original problem.

Most conveniently, each membership certificate of 𝒦2​d\mathcal{K}_{2d} can be written as a matrix positivity condition. Such optimization problems take the form of an SDP, enabling the use of a well developed toolbox for convex optimization. We note here that, in contrast, checking membership of 𝒦\mathcal{K} is computationally intractable, as no efficient numerical methods are known for this task.

It has been shown in [43], see also [49, 17], that under the Archimedean condition this series of upper bounds {λd}dm​i​n∞\{\lambda_{d}\}_{d_{min}}^{\infty} converges asymptotically, i.e., λ∞=λmax\lambda_{\infty}=\lambda_{\max}. However, there are instances where the relaxations converge at a finite order, i.e., ∃d∈ℕ:λd=λmax\exists d\in\mathbb{N}:\lambda_{d}=\lambda_{\max}, where the occurrence is tied to a so-called flatness or rank loop condition on the moment matrix. For a more detailed discussion of the theory of non-commutative semidefinite relaxations, the reader is directed to [12].

Now, many problems naturally occurring in quantum theory exhibit polynomial equality constraints. One can make use of this fact to significantly reduce the size of the underlying SDP by working over the associated quotient space, e.g. comparing equivalence classes up to the constraining equality relations: Let ℐ={∑ivihiwi|vi,wi∈𝕂⟨X¯⟩;hi∈H}\mathcal{I}=\left\{\sum_{i}v_{i}h_{i}w_{i}\,|\,v_{i},w_{i}\in\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle;h_{i}\in H\right\} denote the polynomial two-sided ideal generated by HH. Given a monomial order, any polynomial can be reduced to its unique equivalence class modulo the generators of the ideal. The resulting polynomial is called the normal form 𝒩⁡(⋅)\mathcal{N}(\cdot) of the original one, where the set of normal forms of monomials in 𝕂​⟨X¯⟩\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle forms a canonical basis of the quotient space 𝕂​⟨X¯⟩/ℐ\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle/\mathcal{I}. It is then sufficient to optimize only over said equivalence classes in the degree-dd truncation of the quotient algebra, 𝕂​⟨X¯⟩d/ℐ\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle_{d}/\mathcal{I}:

s.t.λ​1−f=∑ifi∗​fi+∑i,jui​j∗​gi​ui​jmod​ℐ,\displaystyle\,\,\,\,\,\mathrm{s.t.}\quad\lambda{1}-f=\sum_{i}f_{i}^{*}f_{i}+\sum_{i,j}u_{ij}^{*}g_{i}u_{ij}\quad\mathrm{mod}\,\mathcal{I},
deg⁡(fi)≤d,deg⁡(ui​j)≤⌊d−deg⁡(gi)2⌋:=di.\displaystyle\qquad\mathrm{deg}(f_{i})\leq d,\,\,\mathrm{deg}(u_{ij})\leq\left\lfloor\frac{d-\mathrm{deg}(g_{i})}{2}\right\rfloor:=d_{i}.

As many problems native to quantum theory exclusively feature equality constraints, we are going to restrict the following illustration to the case of no inequalities, G=∅G=\emptyset, for now.

To make the SDP underlying (8) more apparent, define a monomial basis vdv_{d} of 𝕂​⟨X¯⟩d/ℐ\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle_{d}/\mathcal{I}, with cardinality denoted by sn,dℐs_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}}. The problem can then be phrased as an optimization over PSD Gram matrices G0∈𝕂sn,dℐ×sn,dℐG_{0}\in\mathbb{K}^{s_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}}\times s_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}}}:

λd=infλ∈ℝ,G0∈𝕂sn,dℐ×sn,dℐλ\displaystyle\lambda_{d}=\inf_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R},G_{0}\in\mathbb{K}^{s_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}}\times s_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}}}}\qquad\lambda (9)
s.t.λ​1−f=vd∗​G0​vdmod​ℐ,\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\,\,\,\,\mathrm{s.t.}\qquad\lambda{1}-f=v_{d}^{*}G_{0}v_{d}\quad\mathrm{mod}\,\mathcal{I},
G0⪰0,\displaystyle\,\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad G_{0}\succeq 0,

where the unconstrained case is recovered by working over the trivial ideal ℐ=∅\mathcal{I}=\emptyset. The optimization can be interpreted as follows: Some of the monomial coefficients of ff predetermine entries of G0G_{0}, while others are undetermined. When running the numerical SDP solver, it attempts to find the best pair (λ,G0)(\lambda,G_{0}) in the intersection of the PSD cone with the affine subspace spanned by the coefficients of λ−f⁡(X¯)\lambda-f(\underline{X}).

The size of PSD matrices in the hierarchy grows exponentially in dd, where in the unconstrained case it reads as

sn,d=dim⁡(𝕂​⟨X¯⟩d)=nd+1−1n−1,s_{n,d}=\mathrm{dim}\left(\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle_{d}\right)=\frac{n^{d+1-1}}{n-1}, (10)

which in general leads to only lower relaxation levels being numerically addressable. For constrained problems, working in the quotient algebra of dimension dim⁡(𝕂​⟨X¯⟩d/ℐ)=sn,dℐ<sn,d\mathrm{dim}\left(\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle_{d}\right/\mathcal{I})=s_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}}<s_{n,d} often reduces the matrix sizes drastically. As mentioned earlier, improving the scalability of the NPA hierarchy, and SDPs in general is an active field of research, where the interested reader is directed to [38] for a survey on scalability improvements by sparsity exploitation.

It is also possible to study this problem on its dual side, optimizing over the set of quantum moments rather than non-negative polynomials [43, 49]. In that setting, the moment matrix replaces the Gram matrix as the central PSD variable. Although the dual viewpoint is often used in the literature, we restrict our discussion to the primal side, as it is the more natural setting for algebraic certification. Note also that the works [43, 49] follow the opposite convention when defining the primal and dual problem.

While the above framework can be used to address generic non-commutative optimization problems of the form (2), polynomial optimization does not constitute the exclusive use of SDPs in quantum theory. SDPs naturally occur, not exhaustively, in applications such as entanglement detection through the Doherty-Parrilo-Spedalieri hierarchy [18], the quantum marginal problem [58], tomography problems [14], or quantum network correlations [50]. In many cases, the SDP structure of the problem arises from the PSD nature of the underlying quantum states or measurements.

3 Extracting certified bounds

As anticipated in Section 1, SDP solvers aiming to certify non-negativity of λ−f\lambda-f via the numerical tuple (λ,G0)(\lambda,G_{0}) might issue inaccurate solutions due to several reasons, such as inexact termination, failure of strict feasibility, or poor conditioning of the problem. Although in theory SDPs are exactly solvable by quantifier elimination [2], this method has doubly exponential complexity in the number of variables [10]. In contrast, if only approximate solutions are required, SDPs can be solved in polynomial time using convex optimization methods such as the ellipsoid or interior-point algorithms [44]. Since scalability is crucial for many problems in quantum theory, this work focuses on post-processing of the numerical data rather than aiming for exact solutions of the underlying SDPs.

Various works discuss the appropriate handling of obtaining exact Sum-of-Squares (SOS) decompositions from inexact data. For univariate polynomials with real or complex coefficients, there are dedicated algorithms approximating complex roots of perturbed positive polynomials [34, 33], or solving norm equations together with using Euler’s identity [29]. In the multivariate case, one can either rely on the so-called rounding and projection [48] (see also [26]) or perturbation-compensation algorithms [37], implemented in the RealCertify package [36]. For constrained compact problems, one can apply rigorous interval arithmetic techniques to obtain a certified upper bound [32]. Similarly to that setting, tailored methods to obtain certified bounds to SDP relaxations to the optimal power-flow problems have been presented in [45]. Related computer-assisted proof techniques have also been used in quantum information to certify finite-dimensional SDP bounds for specific problem instances, for example in channel-discrimination problems, by projecting numerical SDP solutions onto affine matrix constraints and restoring positivity [8]. In contrast, our method aims to extract certified solutions to a wider range of problems, encompassing any problem following the general NPO formulation (2). Other algorithms have been designed for specific problems with finitely many minimizers [35, 7]. Such methods provide exact, rational SOS decompositions, together with a certified rational upper bound of the problem solution. If one is interested in certifying global optimality, one can rely on the recently developed high-precision solver [31] that provides exact SOS decompositions, possibly with non-rational coefficients. On the other hand, if one primarily seeks highly accurate numerical bounds rather than exact certificates, one may use arbitrary-precision SDP solvers (e.g., SDPA-GMP [41]) at the expense of a larger computational cost. However, the output remains a numerical approximation and does not constitute a proof unless further validated by an adequate certification method. The rounding and projection algorithm also has been extended to unconstrained non-commutative problems in [13] to obtain exact rational SOHS decompositions. Our main algorithmic contribution is based on this rounding and projection scheme, in order to handle constraints for maximal eigenvalue problems, as well as sparse/symmetric input data.

Our method offers a complementary guarantee in situations where rigorous bounds to a given problem are of primary interest, independently of the convergence of the original problem.

We now present our constructive procedure that converts an approximate numerical SDP solution of Problem (9) into a formally exact rational certificate. Starting with the case of an unconstrained NPO (G=H=ℐ=∅)(G=H=\mathcal{I}=\emptyset) let (λd,G0)(\lambda_{d},G_{0}) be the numerical tuple of upper bound λd∈ℝ\lambda_{d}\in\mathbb{R} and Gram matrix G0∈𝕂sn,d×sn,dG_{0}\in\mathbb{K}^{s_{n,d}\times s_{n,d}}, as issued by the SDP solver of one’s choice. The left hand side (LHS) LdL_{d} of the numerical certificate at order dd, suggesting λd>λmax\lambda_{d}>\lambda_{\max} then reads

Ld:=λd​1−f≈vd∗​G0​vd.L_{d}:=\lambda_{d}{1}-f\approx v_{d}^{*}G_{0}v_{d}. (11)

The method to obtain an exact certificate from (11) consists of three algebraic steps: (1) rounding of the floating point data to rationally represented data in ℚ\mathbb{Q} with controlled denominator, (2) projection, and (3) lifting, each preserving or restoring feasibility within the truncated quadratic module 𝒦2​d\mathcal{K}_{2d}. After the rounding step, the algebraic operations are performed using exact rational arithmetic, so that no additional round-off error is introduced. A geometric picture of the procedure is displayed in Figure 1. After the first two steps, rounding and projection, the solver’s tuple (λd,G0)(\lambda_{d},G_{0}) has been mapped onto the affine subspace ℒ\mathcal{L} consistent with the coefficients of λd​1−f\lambda_{d}{1}-f, thereby enforcing exact equality in Eq. (11). We call the obtained tuple (𝒫⁡(G~0),λ~d)(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}),\tilde{\lambda}_{d}) a pre-certificate. In the case that 𝒫⁡(G~0)⪰0\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})\succeq 0, we established a proper SOHS certificate, proving λ~d\tilde{\lambda}_{d} as an exact upper bound. If the resulting matrix 𝒫⁡(G~0)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}) is not PSD, in step (3) we lift it back into the PSD cone by adding a rational correction justified by the constraint structure. This lifted matrix 𝒫+​(G~0)\mathcal{P}_{+}(\tilde{G}_{0}) then certifies a weaker bound λdrat>λ~d\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{rat}}>\tilde{\lambda}_{d}, which holds exactly. That is, step (3) is only necessary if 𝒫⁡(G~0)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}) is not PSD. However, in some situations, one can still apply step (3) when 𝒫⁡(G~0)⪰0\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})\succeq 0 to further tighten the bound λ~d\tilde{\lambda}_{d}, as it is shown later.

In the rest of the section, we provide a rigorous formulation of the three steps in the process, both for problems with and without equalities.

3.1 Round and Project

To obtain a nearby rational tuple (𝒫⁡(G~0),λ~d)(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}),\tilde{\lambda}_{d}) from their floating-point counterparts in the unconstrained case, one can make use of the Round and Project procedure from [13]: Fix a given rounding precision η\eta and start by rounding the floating-point data (λd,G0)(\lambda_{d},G_{0}) entry-wise to rational representations (λ~d,G~0)(\tilde{\lambda}_{d},\tilde{G}_{0}), where established methods such as continued fractions can be used. This rounding step should be understood as a reconstruction of adequate rational representations of the floating-point numbers: every floating-point number already represents an exact rational number, and one could in principle use this exact representation directly in all subsequent exact computations. We instead reconstruct a nearby rational number of controlled precision in order to suppress insignificant numerical noise and to avoid unnecessarily large numerators and denominators in the subsequent exact rational arithmetic operations.

Once the reconstructed data (λ~d,G~0)(\widetilde{\lambda}_{d},\widetilde{G}_{0}) have been chosen, the subsequent algebraic projection and lifting operations are performed exactly over the rational coefficient field to not introduce any additional round-off error. Using exact arithmetic instead of floating-point arithmetic is hence crucial for the algebraic manipulation to preserve the exactness of the certificate in intermediate manipulation steps. In the rest of the work, A~\tilde{A} represents the entrywise rationalized form of the object AA, where rationalization on polynomials is understood as acting on their coefficient vector in the monomial basis. We denote by ℚ\mathbb{Q} the rational subfield of 𝕂\mathbb{K} and by ℚ​⟨X¯⟩\mathbb{Q}\langle\underline{X}\rangle the associated rational polynomial algebra (real or complex).

Now, as mentioned earlier, since ff is assumed to have rational coefficients, it constrains the entries of G0G_{0} corresponding to its support. To recover this relationship after rounding, one has to project the entries of G~0\tilde{G}_{0} back into the affine space ℒ\mathcal{L} defined through the coefficients of L~d:=λ~d​1−f\tilde{L}_{d}:=\tilde{\lambda}_{d}{1}-f via [13]:

𝒫​(G~0)α,β=(G~0)α,β−1n⁡(α,β)​∑γ∗​δ∼α∗​β(G~0)γ,δ−(L~d)α∗​β,\displaystyle\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})_{\alpha,\beta}=(\tilde{G}_{0})_{\alpha,\beta}-\frac{1}{n(\alpha,\beta)}\sum_{\gamma^{*}\delta\sim\alpha^{*}\beta}(\tilde{G}_{0})_{\gamma,\delta}-(\tilde{L}_{d})_{\alpha^{*}\beta}, (12)

which can be expressed compactly with a rational correction matrix Δ\Delta as 𝒫⁡(G~0)=G~0+Δ\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})=\tilde{G}_{0}+\Delta. The tuple (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) refers to the indexing with respect to monomials α,β∈𝕂​⟨X¯⟩d\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle_{d}, and pα∗​βp_{\alpha^{*}\beta} refers to the monomial coefficient of α∗​β\alpha^{*}\beta in pp. Intuitively, this projection enforces exact algebraic consistency between the rounded Gram matrix and the target polynomial by averaging over equivalent monomial pairs. Here, n⁡(α,β)n(\alpha,\beta) accounts for the number of such pairs:

n⁡(α,β)={(γ,δ)|γ∗​δ=α∗​β}.n(\alpha,\beta)=\{(\gamma,\delta)\,|\,\gamma^{*}\delta=\alpha^{*}\beta\}. (13)

When considering problems with equalilty constraints, this projection can be adapted by working over the quotient algebra 𝕂​⟨X¯⟩/ℐ\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle/\mathcal{I} by enforcing coefficient equality of normal forms 𝒩⁡(α∗​β)\mathcal{N}(\alpha^{*}\beta) of monomials α∗​β\alpha^{*}\beta, i.e., their equivalence classes in the quotient algebra. The goal is again to find a correction matrix Δ\Delta such that the corrected certificate holds exactly up to normal form reductions

𝒩⁡(L~d)=𝒩⁡(vd∗​(G~0+Δ)​vd).\mathcal{N}(\tilde{L}_{d})=\mathcal{N}\left(v_{d}^{*}(\tilde{G}_{0}+\Delta)v_{d}\right). (14)

As several entries (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) map to the same normal form, there are in general infinitely many ways of constructing Δ\Delta. The most natural choice is the correction with the least Frobenius deviation from the original rationalized Gram matrix: As the numerical Gram matrices are PSD up to the solver precision, deviating the least possible from them will minimize the distance to the PSD cone after projection. The next Lemma provides the formal construction of this projection.

Lemma 2 (Frobenius optimal Gram projection).

For a given optimization problem (9), let α∗​β\alpha^{*}\beta be the monomials corresponding to the basis elements (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) of the Gram matrix G0G_{0}. By construction, they form a basis of 𝕂​⟨X¯⟩2​d\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle_{2d}. Let tt index the basis of equivalence classes in 𝕂​⟨X¯⟩2​d/ℐ\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle_{2d}/\mathcal{I}. The associated normal form operation can then be expressed as

𝒩:𝕂​⟨X¯⟩2​d\displaystyle\mathcal{N}:\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle_{2d} →𝕂​⟨X¯⟩2​d/ℐ\displaystyle\rightarrow\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle_{2d}/\mathcal{I} (15)
α∗​β\displaystyle\alpha^{*}\beta ↦∑tnα,βt​t\displaystyle\mapsto\sum_{t}n_{\alpha,\beta}^{t}t

where nα,βtn_{\alpha,\beta}^{t} is the coefficient with which the word α∗​β\alpha^{*}\beta reduces to tt under 𝒩\mathcal{N}. Define the rational numerical certificate residual coefficients rtr_{t} per reduced word tt as

rt\displaystyle r_{t} =𝒩​(L~d)t−𝒩​(∑α,βvd,α∗​(G~0)α,β​vd,β)t\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}(\tilde{L}_{d})_{t}-\mathcal{N}\left(\sum_{\alpha,\beta}v_{d,\alpha}^{*}(\tilde{G}_{0})_{\alpha,\beta}v_{d,\beta}\right)_{t}
=𝒩​(L~d)t−∑α,βnα,βt​(G~0)α,β.\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}(\tilde{L}_{d})_{t}-\sum_{\alpha,\beta}n_{\alpha,\beta}^{t}(\tilde{G}_{0})_{\alpha,\beta}. (16)

Let Ξ\Xi be the matrix with entries

(Ξ)t,s:=∑α,βnα,βt​nα,βs.(\Xi)_{t,s}:=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}n_{\alpha,\beta}^{t}n_{\alpha,\beta}^{s}. (17)

If Ξ\Xi is non-singular, the following projection 𝒫⁡(G~)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}) yields exact equality between the left hand side (LHS) and right hand side (RHS) of the SOHS certificate:

𝒫​(G~0)α,β\displaystyle\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})_{\alpha,\beta} =(G~0)α,β+Δα,β\displaystyle=(\tilde{G}_{0})_{\alpha,\beta}+\Delta_{\alpha,\beta}
=(G~0)α,β+∑t(Ξ−1​r)t​nα,βt.\displaystyle=(\tilde{G}_{0})_{\alpha,\beta}+\sum_{t}(\Xi^{-1}r)_{t}n_{\alpha,\beta}^{t}. (18)

Furthermore, it is the optimal projection 𝒫\mathcal{P} in terms of Frobenius deviation

‖𝒫⁡(G~0)−G~0‖F2=∑α,β|(𝒫⁡(G~0)−G~0)α,β|2\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})-\tilde{G}_{0}\|^{2}_{F}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}|\left(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})-\tilde{G}_{0}\right)_{\alpha,\beta}|^{2} (19)

from the rounded numerical Gram matrix G~0\tilde{G}_{0}.

Proof of Lemma 2.

Let the assumptions in Lemma 2 hold. We phrase the problem of finding the correction Δ\Delta with least Frobenius norm as a convex quadratic optimization problem:

infΔ∈ℚsn,dℐ×sn,dℐ12​‖Δ‖F2\displaystyle\inf_{\Delta\in\mathbb{Q}^{s_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}}\times s_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}}}}\frac{1}{2}\|\Delta\|_{F}^{2} (20)
s.t.\displaystyle\mathrm{s.t.}\qquad rt=∑α,βnα,βt​Δα,β,∀t,\displaystyle\quad r_{t}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}n_{\alpha,\beta}^{t}\Delta_{\alpha,\beta},\quad\forall t,

which can be solved using Lagrangian multipliers λt\lambda_{t}. Stationarity of the Lagrangian yields

Δα,β=∑tλt​nα,βt.\Delta_{\alpha,\beta}=\sum_{t}\lambda_{t}n_{\alpha,\beta}^{t}. (21)

Plugging back into the constraints yields

rt=Ξ​λt.r_{t}=\Xi\lambda_{t}. (22)

If Ξ\Xi is non-singular, using (21) and (22) one finds the global optimizer

Δα,β=∑t(Ξ−1​r)t​nα,βt.\Delta_{\alpha,\beta}=\sum_{t}(\Xi^{-1}r)_{t}n_{\alpha,\beta}^{t}. (23)

∎

Now, in many settings, such as Bell inequalities or ground states of quantum many body systems, the equality constraints defining the problem relate two monomials to each other. Hence, the associated normal forms map monomials onto monomials instead of polynomials. We call such normal forms and the associated ideals binomial. In such cases, one finds a diagonal Ξ≻0\Xi\succ 0 and the Frobenius optimal solution always exists:

Corollary 3.

If 𝒩\mathcal{N} is binomial, the Frobenius ideal projection reduces to

𝒫​(G~)α,β=G~α,β+r𝒩⁡(α∗​β)nℐ​(α,β)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G})_{\alpha,\beta}=\tilde{G}_{\alpha,\beta}+\frac{r_{\mathcal{N}(\alpha^{*}\beta)}}{n_{\mathcal{I}}(\alpha,\beta)} (24)

with

nℐ​(α,β)=#⁡{(γ,δ):𝒩⁡(α∗​β)=𝒩⁡(γ∗​δ)}.n_{\mathcal{I}}(\alpha,\beta)=\#\{(\gamma,\delta):\mathcal{N}(\alpha^{*}\beta)=\mathcal{N}(\gamma^{*}\delta)\}. (25)
Proof of Corollary 3.

Binomial normal forms can be expressed as

𝒩:α∗​β↦δ𝒩⁡(α∗​β),t​t\mathcal{N}:\alpha^{*}\beta\mapsto\delta_{\mathcal{N}(\alpha^{*}\beta),t}t (26)

which allows us to rewrite the residuals rtr_{t} as

rt=𝒩(L~d)t−∑α,β:𝒩⁡(α∗​β)=tG~α,β.r_{t}=\mathcal{N}(\tilde{L}_{d})_{t}-\sum_{\alpha,\beta:\mathcal{N}(\alpha^{*}\beta)=t}\tilde{G}_{\alpha,\beta}. (27)

Applying the method of Lagrangian multipliers yields

Δα,β=λt​δ𝒩⁡(α∗​β),t.\Delta_{\alpha,\beta}=\lambda_{t}\delta_{\mathcal{N}(\alpha^{*}\beta),t}. (28)

Plugging this into the constraints yields

rt=∑α,β:𝒩⁡(α∗​β)=tλt⇒λt=rtnℐ​(α,β),r_{t}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta:\mathcal{N}(\alpha^{*}\beta)=t}\lambda_{t}\Rightarrow\lambda_{t}=\frac{r_{t}}{n_{\mathcal{I}}(\alpha,\beta)}, (29)

which, when used with 28, implies the claim. ∎

As (12) is implied by (24), in what follows we are going to restrict our considerations to the quotient case without loss of generality.

The projection formula is also readily adapted to problems featuring inequality constraints. Recall that in that case, the numerical certificate reads

λ​1−f=∑fi∗​fi+∑i,jui​j∗​gi​ui​jmod​ℐ,\lambda{1}-f=\sum f_{i}^{*}f_{i}+\sum_{i,j}u_{ij}^{*}g_{i}u_{ij}\quad\mathrm{mod}\,\mathcal{I}, (30)

which, when expressed through Gram matrices, features one matrix G0G_{0} corresponding to the SOHS ∑ifi∗​fi\sum_{i}f_{i}^{*}f_{i}, and mGm_{G} matrices {Gi}i=1mG\{G_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m_{G}} of sizes sn,diℐs_{n,d_{i}}^{\mathcal{I}} corresponding to the so-called localizing terms ∑i,jui​j∗​gi​ui​j\sum_{i,j}u_{ij}^{*}g_{i}u_{ij}. To deal with such constraints, one adapts the LHS from Equation (11) to feature the inequality terms, and projects the rounded principal Gram matrix G~0\tilde{G}_{0} onto the rationalized LHS as before to match coefficients.

To do so, start by constructing the rational LHS L~d\tilde{L}_{d} featuring the inequality terms:

L~d:=λ~d​1−f−∑i∑ju~i​j∗​gi​u~i,j.\tilde{L}_{d}:=\tilde{\lambda}_{d}{1}-f-\sum_{i}\sum_{j}\tilde{u}_{ij}^{*}g_{i}\tilde{u}_{i,j}. (31)

To obtain the rational polynomials u~i​j\tilde{u}_{ij} in the decomposition, one starts by rounding the floating-point localizing Gram matrices {Gi}i=1mG\{G_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m_{G}} to rationals {G~i}i=1mG\{\tilde{G}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m_{G}}. Afterwards, to obtain a nearby rational PSD Gram matrix, we numerically project G~i\widetilde{G}_{i} onto the PSD cone via an eigendecomposition and rationally reconstruct the resulting factors:

𝒫⁡(G~i)=U~i​U~iT;U~i=V~i​diag​(max⁡(λi​j~,0))\small\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{i})=\tilde{U}_{i}\tilde{U}_{i}^{T};\hskip 9.24994pt\tilde{U}_{i}=\tilde{V}_{i}\mathrm{diag}\left(\max(\tilde{\sqrt{\lambda_{ij}}},0)\right) (32)

with V~\tilde{V} being the matrix of rationalized eigenvectors of Gi~\tilde{G_{i}} and {λi​j}j=1,..,sn,di\{\lambda_{ij}\}_{j=1,..,s_{n,d_{i}}} the corresponding numerical eigenvalues. From these, the polynomials u~i​j\tilde{u}_{ij} are obtained as

u~i​j=(U~iT​vdi)j,\tilde{u}_{ij}=(\tilde{U}_{i}^{T}{{v}_{d}}_{i})_{j}, (33)

where vdi{{v}_{d}}_{i} denotes the monomial basis appropriate for the localizing matrix of gig_{i}. Using Lemma 2 to project G~0\tilde{G}_{0} onto L~d\tilde{L}_{d} from Equation (31) yields a pre-certificate L~d=vd∗​𝒫​(G~0)​vd\tilde{L}_{d}=v_{d}^{*}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})v_{d}, and with 𝒫⁡(G~0)⪰0\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})\succeq 0 it would certify membership of λ~d​1−f\tilde{\lambda}_{d}{1}-f in 𝒦2​d\mathcal{K}_{2d} and hence λ~d\tilde{\lambda}_{d} as an upper bound to ff. This procedure also applies to moment inequality constraints of the form ⟨mi⟩≥0\langle m_{i}\rangle\geq 0, where the associated multiplier polynomials u~i​j\tilde{u}_{ij} are scalar valued (degree 00).

Performing the Round and Project procedure, in the unconstrained or constrained case, results in an exact pre-certificate

L~d=vd∗​𝒫​(G0~)​vdmod​ℐ,\tilde{L}_{d}=v_{d}^{*}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G_{0}})v_{d}\quad\mathrm{mod}\,\mathcal{I}, (34)

where this expression constitutes an exact algebraic identity, ensuring that any remaining infeasibility stems solely from the non-positivity of 𝒫⁡(G~0)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}).

As anticipated, in the best case, the resulting projected Gram matrix 𝒫⁡(G0~)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G_{0}}) is already PSD. This can only be the case if the rounded bound λ~d\tilde{\lambda}_{d} is a valid upper bound to the global optimum, λ~d≥λmax\tilde{\lambda}_{d}\geq\lambda_{\max}, and hence leaves us with the certified bound λ~d\tilde{\lambda}_{d}.

3.2 Lifting positivity

The remaining question is how to repair a pre-certificate (34) whose Gram matrix was projected out of the PSD cone, rendering it vacuous. This particularly happens if λ~d≱λmax\tilde{\lambda}_{d}\ngeq\lambda_{\max}. The next Theorem provides, under reasonably mild assumptions, an explicit, constraint-dependent lifting that guarantees a valid upper bound.

Theorem 4 (Certified bounds to NPOs).

Let 𝒫⁡(G~0)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}) be the rounded and projected Gram matrix obtained from Lemma 2 with μmin∈ℚ\mu_{\mathrm{min}}\in\mathbb{Q} a lower bound to its spectrum, and let sn,dℐs^{\mathcal{I}}_{n,d} denote the number of monomials in nn variables up to degree dd after normal form reduction. Assume that the underlying variables X¯\underline{X} are subject to one of the following polynomial constraints:

  • •

    Ball constraints: 1⪰∑iXi21\succeq\sum_{i}X_{i}^{2},

  • •

    Box constraints: 1−Xi2⪰0​∀i1-X_{i}^{2}\succeq 0\,\,\forall i,

  • •

    Unipotency: 1−Xi2=0​∀i1-X_{i}^{2}=0\,\,\forall i,

  • •

    Projection constraints: Xi2=Xi​∀iX_{i}^{2}=X_{i}\,\,\forall i,

then, the rational bound λdrat∈ℚ\lambda^{\mathrm{rat}}_{d}\in\mathbb{Q} with

λdrat:=λ~d+δd;δd:=−min{μmin,0}⋅sn,dℐ\lambda^{\mathrm{rat}}_{d}:=\tilde{\lambda}_{d}+\delta_{d};\quad\delta_{d}:=-\min\{\mu_{\mathrm{min}},0\}\cdot s^{\mathcal{I}}_{n,d} (35)

constitutes a certified upper bound to the optimization problem, i.e., λdrat≥λmax\lambda^{\mathrm{rat}}_{d}\geq\lambda_{\max}.

Importantly, the condition on the existence of constraints is rather weak: In the non-locality scenario, Bell type expressions can be defined in terms of projectors, while in the quantum many-body setting, the underlying local spin operators naturally fulfill unipotency.

The geometric intuition behind the proof of Theorem 4 is that the non-PSD Gram matrix 𝒫⁡(G~0)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}) is lifted by adding a multiple of the identity to the certificate, leading to a weaker bound λrat\lambda^{\mathrm{rat}}. The allowed correction magnitude is guaranteed to be feasible within the quadratic module due to the following Lemma.

Lemma 5 (Constant SOHS decomposition).

Let ε>0\varepsilon>0. If the variables X¯\underline{X} are subject to constraints as in Theorem 4, one can find the following exact, constant SOHS decomposition

ε​sn,dℐ​1=ε​vd∗​vd+∑krk∗​rk+∑iqk​i∗​ci​qk​imod​ℐ\varepsilon s^{\mathcal{I}}_{n,d}{1}=\varepsilon v_{d}^{*}v_{d}+\sum_{k}r_{k}^{*}r_{k}+\sum_{i}q_{ki}^{*}c_{i}q_{ki}\quad\mathrm{mod}\,\mathcal{I} (36)

for some rk,qk​i∈ℚ​⟨X¯⟩dr_{k},q_{ki}\in\mathbb{Q}\langle\underline{X}\rangle_{d} and vdv_{d} the monomial basis of 𝕂​⟨X¯⟩d/ℐ\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle_{d}/\mathcal{I}.

Lemma 5 can be proven by induction, as shown in Appendix A. Using this, we can prove Theorem 4:

Proof of Theorem 4.

Let the assumptions in Theorem 4 hold. We are going to show that for λrat\lambda^{\mathrm{rat}} there exists some PSD gram matrix 𝒫+​(G~0)\mathcal{P}_{+}(\tilde{G}_{0}) and polynomials pi​jp_{ij} such that

λrat​1−f\displaystyle\lambda^{\mathrm{rat}}{1}-f =vd∗(𝒫+(G~0))vd+∑i,jpi​j∗gipi​jmodℐ\displaystyle=v_{d}^{*}\left(\mathcal{P}_{+}(\tilde{G}_{0})\right)v_{d}+\sum_{i,j}p_{ij}^{*}g_{i}p_{ij}\qquad\mathrm{mod}\,\mathcal{I}
⇔λrat​1−f∈𝒦2​d,\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\lambda^{\mathrm{rat}}{1}-f\in\mathcal{K}_{2d}, (37)

which implies the claim.

Consider the exact pre-certificate (34). If μmin<0\mu_{\mathrm{min}}<0 then adding (36) with ε=−μmin\varepsilon=-\mu_{\min} to both sides of the certificate lifts 𝒫⁡(G~0)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}) back into the PSD cone as follows:

λ~d​1−μmin​sn,dℐ​1−f−∑i,ju~i​j∗​gi​u~i​j\displaystyle\tilde{\lambda}_{d}{1}-\mu_{\min}s^{\mathcal{I}}_{n,d}{1}-f-\sum_{i,j}\tilde{u}^{*}_{ij}g_{i}\tilde{u}_{ij} (38)
=vd∗​(𝒫⁡(G~0)−μmin​1)​vd+∑krk∗​rk+∑i,kqk​i∗​ci​qk​i.\displaystyle=v_{d}^{*}\left(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})-\mu_{\min}{1}\right)v_{d}+\sum_{k}r_{k}^{*}r_{k}+\sum_{i,k}q_{ki}^{*}c_{i}q_{ki}.

Intuitively, this addition corresponds to lifting the spectrum of 𝒫⁡(G~0)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}) by −μmin>0-\mu_{\min}>0 while staying within the quadratic module, thereby restoring positivity without changing the algebraic identity of the certificate.

Expressing the rkr_{k} contributions with a PSD matrix R0R_{0} of the same size, and joining terms corresponding to constraints cic_{i} yields

λ~d​1−μmin​sn,dℐ​1−f\displaystyle\tilde{\lambda}_{d}{1}-\mu_{\min}s^{\mathcal{I}}_{n,d}{1}-f =vd∗​(𝒫⁡(G~0)−μmin​1+R0)​vd\displaystyle=v_{d}^{*}\left(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})-\mu_{\min}{1}+R_{0}\right)v_{d}
+∑i,jpi​j∗gipi​j,\displaystyle+\sum_{i,j}p_{ij}^{*}g_{i}p_{ij}, (39)

which implies the claim with

𝒫+​(G~0)=(𝒫⁡(G~0)−μmin​1+R0)\mathcal{P}_{+}(\tilde{G}_{0})=\left(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})-\mu_{\min}{1}+R_{0}\right) (40)

depending on the constraints involved. ∎

It should be noted that a numerical bound may have been correct even if the corresponding Gram matrix G0G_{0} is projected outside the PSD cone. Consequently, our method allows one to (a) recover valid bounds from possibly incorrect ones, and (b) validate correct bounds, but it does not provide a necessary certificate of invalidity for numerical bounds.

The above argument only holds if μmin\mu_{\min} actually constitutes a rigorous lower bound to the spectrum of 𝒫⁡(G~0)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}). Unfortunately, the Abel-Ruffini theorem implies no closed form solution for the eigenvalues of generic square matrices of dimension larger than four, as they are defined as the roots of the associated characteristic polynomial. A rigorous lower bound on the smallest eigenvalue can instead be obtained using certified interval arithmetic. In our implementation, Arblib.jl [25] performs arbitrary-precision floating-point ball arithmetic, yielding an interval guaranteed to contain a given eigenvalue. The certified lower endpoint of this enclosure constitutes a certified lower bound to the eigenspectrum. Since this endpoint is a finite binary floating-point number, we use its exact rational representation in the subsequent algebraic computations. As the floating-point bound is already certified and holds exactly, its exact rational representation can be used while maintaining validity throughout. We emphasize that the working precision of Arblib controls the tightness of the eigenvalue enclosure, but not the validity of the certification. Throughout this work, all eigenvalue bounds entering the certification procedure are understood in this rigorous sense.

Theorem 4 establishes that any numerical non-negativity certificate returned by an SDP solver can be transformed into an exact rational bound by a finite algebraic correction depending on the minimal eigenvalue defect and the problem size. An important observation is that the bound correction term δd=−min{μmin,0}⋅sn,dℐ\delta_{d}=-\min\{\mu_{\min},0\}\cdot s^{\mathcal{I}}_{n,d} is affected by two factors, (i) the distance from the projected 𝒫⁡(G~0)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}) to the PSD cone, and (ii) the size of the problem in terms of variables and relaxation order. While working with high precision solvers and rounding arithmetic can lead to smaller distances to the PSD cone, the term sn,dℐs^{\mathcal{I}}_{n,d} ultimately dominates the bound correction, as it will be illustrated in later sections.

3.3 Bound tightening of interior pre-certificates

Now, in the case of the projected Gram matrix being positive-definite (PD), e.g. 𝒫⁡(G~0)≻0\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})\succ 0, it is not necessary to perform the lifting step to restore feasibility. However, it is possible to leverage the positive eigenspectrum to obtain a tighter bound λdrat<λ~d\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{rat}}<\tilde{\lambda}_{d} by shifting the PSD matrix closer to the boundary of its cone. This can be done in two ways, (1) in the presence of unipotency constraints Xi2=1X_{i}^{2}=1, one can use a modification of Lemma 5 with ε<0\varepsilon<0, while in the other cases one can make use of a rank-1 PSD downgrade, as explained in the next Lemma.

Theorem 6 (Certified tightening for interior pre-certificates).

Assume that the Frobenius optimal projection 2 leads to 𝒫⁡(G~0)≻0\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})\succ 0 lying in the interior of the PSD cone. Let μmin>0\mu_{\min}>0 be a certified lower bound to the spectrum, and let

τ=1e0∗​𝒫​(G~0)−1​e0\tau=\frac{1}{e_{0}^{*}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})^{-1}e_{0}} (41)

where e0∈𝕂sn,dℐe_{0}\in\mathbb{K}^{s_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}}} denotes the coordinate vector selecting the constant monomial s.t. e0∗​vd=1e_{0}^{*}v_{d}=1. Then, a tighter bound λdrat<λ~d\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{rat}}<\tilde{\lambda}_{d} can be obtained depending on the constraints involved:

(i) If the variables are subject to unipotency constraints, {1−Xi2}⊆H\{1-X_{i}^{2}\}\subseteq H, then λdrat=λ~d−μmin⋅sn,dℐ\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{rat}}=\tilde{\lambda}_{d}-\mu_{\min}\cdot s_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}} constitutes a rigorous upper bound to the optimization problem

(ii) Independently of the constraints, λdrat=λ~d−τ\lambda^{\mathrm{rat}}_{d}=\tilde{\lambda}_{d}-\tau constitutes a rigorous upper bound to the optimization problem, where τ∈[μmin,μmax]\tau\in[\mu_{\min},\mu_{\max}] with μmax\mu_{\max} an upper bound to the spectrum of 𝒫⁡(G~0).\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}).

The proof for this Theorem can be found in Appendix B. Applying this Theorem in the case of 𝒫⁡(G~0)≻0\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})\succ 0 lets one further tighten the numerical rounded bounds while certifying them. Note that as the numerical optima of the SDP lie on the boundary of the PSD cone, in the generic case the eigenspectrum of 𝒫⁡(G~0)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}) is not positive as the Frobenius distance between 𝒫⁡(G~0)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}) and G~0\tilde{G}_{0} is minimized. However, in numerically delicate instances where PSD solvers terminate in the interior of the cone, the above scenario does occur, as it is observed and interpreted in Section 6. Also note that in the case of unipotency constraints one can apply either of the two tightening strategies, while procedure (i) carries an extra factor sn,dℐs_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}} which, for large problems, will typically result in a tighter bound than procedure (ii).

Concludingly, we established a rigorous method to obtain mathematical non-negativity proof from the solver’s data and presented an adapted method for interior solutions where the algorithm provides certified bounds tighter than their numerical counterpart.

The same above reasoning of rounding, projecting, and lifting, can be extended to structured relaxations such as sparsity or symmetry-adapted hierarchies, as presented in the next section.

4 Exact certificates under sparsity and symmetry

There exist problem for which it is necessary to go to higher orders of the hierarchy to get tight bounds to the solution of the optimization problem. In those cases, the exponential growth of the PSD matrices with the relaxation order often makes higher intractable in practice, especially if a large number of variables is involved. This bottleneck of semidefinite relaxations is of particular importance, for instance, in quantum many-body physics, as one is often interested in the behavior of systems of large sizes. One way to be able to address such problems, is to employ a sparse version of the hierarchy, which relies on a sparse analogue of Theorem 1. Applying the sparse instead of the standard, dense hierarchy has led to improvements in scalability by orders of magnitude, if the problem admits certain structure [54, 55]. In other cases, the symmetry of the problem can be exploited to achieve a block-diagonal form of the Gram matrix and thus reducing computational complexity. In this section, we adapt the procedure described above to get rigorous bounds for systems that are sparse or symmetric. First, we will focus on the sparse case.

4.1 Hierarchies for sparse systems

We start by giving a brief introduction to correlative sparsity and the associated SOHS hierarchy. The idea is that one can exploit a sparse correlation pattern of the variables, to then construct several, smaller Gram (or moment) matrices, indexed by cliques of variables that correlate among each other. This is in stark contrast to the dense hierarchy, where a single PSD block is indexed by monomials between all variables in the problem. Employing the sparse hierarchy leads to more PSD conditions of smaller sizes instead of one larger one. As the dominant computational cost for SDP solvers arises from the largest block in the PSD conditions, employing methods to reduce its dimension is crucial to improve the efficiency of SDP hierarchies.

To start, build the correlation graph C={V,E}C=\{V,E\} with vertices V=X¯V=\underline{X} given by the operators in the problem, and edges EE between them whenever they occur together multiplicatively in the support of the objective ff, or additively in the constraints in GG, and HH.

The next step to obtain the hierarchy consists in preprocessing the correlation graph CC: A chordal graph is a graph in which every cycle of length k≥4k\geq 4 contains a chord, i.e., an edge joining two non-adjacent vertices of the cycle. An important fact is that every non-chordal graph can be extended to be chordal by adding edges to EE, which is called a chordal extension. Note that there is often more than one way to render a given correlation graph chordal.

After performing the chordal extension, one identifies the so-called maximal cliques in the graph: A clique is a subset Ck⊂VC_{k}\subset V such that every pair Xi,Xj∈CkX_{i},X_{j}\in C_{k} satisfies (i,j)∈E(i,j)\in E, which is called maximal if no other clique Ck′C_{k}^{\prime} with Ck⊊Ck′C_{k}\subsetneq C_{k}^{\prime} exists. As an example, in Figure 2 (b)(b), the maximal cliques can be identified as C1={X1,X2,X3}C_{1}=\{X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}\}, C2={X1,X3,X4}C_{2}=\{X_{1},X_{3},X_{4}\}, and C3={X1,X5}C_{3}=\{X_{1},X_{5}\}. When opting for the chordal extension (c)(c) instead, one can identify the two cliques C1={X1,X2,X3,X4}C_{1}=\{X_{1},X_{2},X_{3},X_{4}\} and C2={X1,X5}C_{2}=\{X_{1},X_{5}\}. We note here that, by construction of the correlation graph, each constraint features variables from a single clique. Hence, we define Jk⊆[mG]J_{k}\subseteq[m_{G}] as the set of indices ii of inequality constraints contained in CkC_{k}. Furthermore, let NCN_{C} denote the number of maximal cliques, nk=|Ck|n_{k}=|C_{k}| the cardinality of the clique, and 𝕂​⟨Ck¯⟩\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{C_{k}}\rangle the ∗*-algebra spanned by CkC_{k}.

Having constructed the chordal extension and identified the maximal cliques, one can define the dd-th relaxation level of the sparse SOHS hierarchy:

λdsp=infλ∈ℝ,fk,ℓ,ui​j(k)∈𝕂⁡⟨Ck¯⟩/ℐλ\displaystyle\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{sp}}=\inf_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R},\,f_{k,\ell},\,u^{(k)}_{ij}\in\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{C_{k}}\rangle/\mathcal{I}}\qquad\lambda (42)
s.t.λ1−f=\displaystyle\quad\,\,\,\,\mathrm{s.t.}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\lambda{1}-f=
∑k=1Nc(∑ℓfk,ℓ∗​fk,ℓ+∑i∈Jk∑j(ui​j(k))∗​gi​ui​j(k))​mod​ℐ\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{N_{c}}\left(\sum_{\ell}f_{k,\ell}^{*}f_{k,\ell}\;+\;\sum_{i\in J_{k}}\sum_{j}(u^{(k)}_{ij})^{*}\,g_{i}\,u^{(k)}_{ij}\right)\,\,\mathrm{mod}\,\mathcal{I}
deg⁡(fk,ℓ)≤d,deg⁡(ui​j(k))≤⌊d−deg⁡(gi)2⌋.\displaystyle\,\,\qquad\mathrm{deg}(f_{k,\ell})\leq d,\,\,\mathrm{deg}\!\left(u^{(k)}_{ij}\right)\leq\left\lfloor\frac{d-\mathrm{deg}(g_{i})}{2}\right\rfloor.

Similarly to the dense hierarchy 8, the first condition characterizes membership in the associated sparse truncated quadratic module, which according to the sparse version [27] of Theorem 1 certifies positivity on KK. The main difference to the dense case is that the SOHS splits over contributions per clique, i.e., summands fk,lf_{k,l} and ui,j(k)u_{i,j}^{(k)} stemming from the clique-wise algebras 𝕂​⟨Ck¯⟩/ℐ\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{C_{k}}\rangle/\mathcal{I}. Hence, when expressing the SOHS in terms of PSD Gram matrices, one is left with NCN_{C} principal Gram matrices G0(k)G_{0}^{(k)} indexed by the variables in CkC_{k}, as well as mGm_{G} localizing-type Gram matrices associated to the ui​j(k)u_{ij}^{(k)}, equivalently indexed by variables from CkC_{k}. This manifests the anticipated reduction in the maximal PSD block size by employing the sparse hierarchy.

As mentioned, for a given correlations graph, there are different ways of constructing chordal extensions, which eventually introduces a tradeoff between computational complexity (smaller cliques) and tightness of the relaxation (larger cliques). Depending on the chosen chordal extension of the correlation graph, one obtains PSD constraints on larger or smaller blocks, where the dense hierarchy 8 is recovered in the case of a single clique C1=X¯C_{1}=\underline{X}. This introduces a second dimension to the hierarchy, i.e., the degree of the chordal extension, where more complete graphs are associated to larger computational complexity while providing tighter bounds. Intuitively, allowing for SOHS summands from a bigger space might let one find more elaborate expressions to certify a tighter bound. It has been shown in [27] that in the case of a chordal extension, one recovers the dense asymptotic convergence results, λ∞sp=λmax\lambda_{\infty}^{\mathrm{sp}}=\lambda_{\max}. However, at each finite relaxation order, the dense bounds lower bound the sparse bounds, λd≤λdsp\lambda_{d}\leq\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{sp}}.

4.2 Exact certificates for sparse systems

Now that we have introduced the numerical sparse SOHS certificates, we are going to establish a rigorous way on how to extract a certified upper bound from the corresponding numerical data. The rounding–projection–lifting strategy developed for the dense hierarchy extends naturally to such relaxations which exploit correlative sparsity. Let the sparse numerical certificate be denoted by the tuple (λdsp,{G0(k)}k=1NC,{Gi(k)}i=1mG)(\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{sp}},\{G_{0}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{N_{C}},\{G_{i}^{(k)}\}_{i=1}^{m_{G}}).

The numerical certificate (possibly over a quotient space) then reads as

Ld≈∑k(vd(k))∗​G0(k)​vd(k)mod​ℐ,L_{d}\approx\sum_{k}\left(v_{d}^{(k)}\right)^{*}G_{0}^{(k)}v_{d}^{(k)}\quad\mathrm{mod}\,\mathcal{I}, (43)

where vd(k)v_{d}^{(k)} denotes the monomial basis vector of 𝕂​⟨Ck¯⟩d/ℐ\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{C_{k}}\rangle_{d}/\mathcal{I}, and the LHS LdL_{d} includes the inequality localizing contributions Gi(k)G_{i}^{(k)} exactly as in the dense case. The normal form 𝒩\mathcal{N} can then be expressed on the monomial basis of each clique

𝒩:(α,β)k↦∑tnα​β​kt​t,\mathcal{N}:(\alpha,\beta)_{k}\mapsto\sum_{t}n_{\alpha\beta k}^{t}t, (44)

where reductions occur in the global quotient 𝕂​⟨X¯⟩/ℐ\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle/\mathcal{I}, so reduced words tt can receive contributions from multiple cliques. We search again for rational correction matrices Δ(k)\Delta^{(k)} such that the certificate holds exactly for all reduced word coefficients tt:

𝒩​(Ld)t=𝒩​(∑k(vd(k))∗​(G0(k)+Δ(k))​vd(k))t\small\mathcal{N}(L_{d})_{t}=\mathcal{N}\left(\sum_{k}\left(v_{d}^{(k)}\right)^{*}(G_{0}^{(k)}+\Delta^{(k)})v_{d}^{(k)}\right)_{t} (45)

For that, one again defines the residuals per reduced words, now involving Gram matrices associated to all cliques:

rt=𝒩​(Ld)t−∑α,β,knα​β​kt​(G0(k))α,β,r_{t}=\mathcal{N}\left(L_{d}\right)_{t}-\sum_{\alpha,\beta,k}n_{\alpha\beta k}^{t}\left(G_{0}^{(k)}\right)_{\alpha,\beta}, (46)

where (α,β,k)(\alpha,\beta,k) runs over monomial pairs (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) belonging to clique kk. Following exactly the same argument as in Theorem 2 but summing over tuples involving the clique index (α,β,k)(\alpha,\beta,k) let us derive the Frobenius optimal projection in the sparse case.

Lemma 7 (Frobenius optimal sparse Gram projection).

Let (α∗​β)k∈𝕂​⟨X¯⟩2​d(\alpha^{*}\beta)_{k}\in\mathbb{K}\langle\underline{X}\rangle_{2d} be the word corresponding to indices (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) of Gram matrix G0(k)G_{0}^{(k)}. Let

(Ξ)t,s=∑α,β,knα​β​kt​nα​β​ks.(\Xi)_{t,s}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta,k}n_{\alpha\beta k}^{t}n_{\alpha\beta k}^{s}. (47)

If Ξ\Xi is invertible, the Frobenius optimal correction reads

Δα,β(k)=∑t(Ξ−1​r)t​nα​β​kt,\Delta^{(k)}_{\alpha,\beta}=\sum_{t}(\Xi^{-1}r)_{t}n_{\alpha\beta k}^{t}, (48)

where for binomial 𝒩\mathcal{N} the Frobenius optimal correction reads

Δα,β(k)=r𝒩⁡(α∗​β)nℐ​(α,β,k)\Delta^{(k)}_{\alpha,\beta}=\frac{r_{\mathcal{N}(\alpha^{*}\beta)}}{n_{\mathcal{I}}(\alpha,\beta,k)} (49)

with

nℐ​(α,β,k)=#⁡{(γ,δ,l):𝒩⁡((α∗​β)k)=𝒩⁡((γ∗​δ)l)}.\small n_{\mathcal{I}}(\alpha,\beta,k)=\#\{(\gamma,\delta,l):\mathcal{N}((\alpha^{*}\beta)_{k})=\mathcal{N}((\gamma^{*}\delta)_{l})\}. (50)

The proof follows exactly the same argument as the proof of Lemma 2 and is hence not presented here.

Intuitively, this result tells us how to update the entries of Gram matrices associated to different cliques, such that the projected Gram matrices deviate the least from their numerical counterpart. Again, this is a natural choice because we expect the least deviation of the eigenvalues of the numerical Gram matrices, hence minimizing the bound loss associated to our scheme.

In the case of the projected Gram matrices leaving the PSD cone, we perform a similar lifting of λ\lambda as in the dense case, where we again denote the rounded, projected, and lifted matrices with 𝒫+​(G~0(k))\mathcal{P}_{+}(\tilde{G}_{0}^{(k)}).

Theorem 8 (Sparse certified bounds).

Assume an inaccurate numerical certificate (λdsp,{G0(k)}k=1NC,{Gi(k)}i=1mG)(\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{sp}},\{G_{0}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{N_{C}},\{G_{i}^{(k)}\}_{i=1}^{m_{G}}) with the Gram matrices {𝒫⁡(G0(k))}\{\mathcal{P}(G_{0}^{(k)})\} admitting lower spectral bounds μmink\mu^{k}_{\mathrm{min}} after rounding and projecting.
