4.3 Exact certificates for symmetric systems

The structure of the numerical certificate (43) is not exclusive to sparse relaxations, but also occurs in the case of block diagonal Gram matrices G0G_{0}. As block-diagonalizable Gram matrices correspond to associated symmetries, one can adapt Theorem 8 to also be able to obtain certified bounds on symmetry-reduced problems of the corresponding form.

Lemma 9 (Frobenius optimal Gram projection over polynomial bases).

Assume that due to the symmetry of a problem, the underlying Gram matrix G0G_{0} can be block-diagonalized by a transformation UU into KK blocks G0(k)G_{0}^{(k)} of maximal size NN. Depending on UU, each block will be indexed by a non-monomial basis, e.g., polynomials {bi(k)}i=1N\{b_{i}^{(k)}\}_{i=1}^{N}, which can be expressed in the monomial basis of the full space {vα}α=1K​N\{v_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha=1}^{KN}as

bi(k)=∑αbi,α(k)​vα,b_{i}^{(k)}=\sum_{\alpha}b_{i,\alpha}^{(k)}v_{\alpha}, (56)

where bi,α(k)b_{i,\alpha}^{(k)} are the matrix elements of UU. Assuming an ideal ℐ\mathcal{I} generating a normal form expressed on the monomial basis as in (8), the corresponding symmetry-adapted non-negativity certificate reads as

𝒩⁡(f−λ​1)\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(f-\lambda{1}) =𝒩⁡(∑i,j,k(bi(k))∗​Gi​j(k)​bj(k))\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}\left(\sum_{i,j,k}(b_{i}^{(k)})^{*}G_{ij}^{(k)}b_{j}^{(k)}\right) (57)
=∑i,j,k,α,β(bi,α(k))∗​Gi​j(k)​bj,β(k)​𝒩​(vα∗​vβ),\displaystyle=\sum_{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(b_{i,\alpha}^{(k)})^{*}G_{ij}^{(k)}b_{j,\beta}^{(k)}\,\mathcal{N}(v_{\alpha}^{*}v_{\beta}),
𝒩​(f−λ​1)t\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(f-\lambda{1})_{t} =∑i,j,k,α,β(bi,α(k))∗​Gi​j(k)​bj,β(k)​nα​β​kt:=∑i,j,kn~i​j​kt​Gi​j(k),\displaystyle=\sum_{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(b_{i,\alpha}^{(k)})^{*}G_{ij}^{(k)}b_{j,\beta}^{(k)}\,n_{\alpha\beta k}^{t}:=\sum_{i,j,k}\tilde{n}_{ijk}^{t}G_{ij}^{(k)},

which has the same form as in Theorem 8. Defining the matrix Ξ\Xi accordingly, the Frobenius optimal projection for the Gram blocks indexed by polynomial bases is given by

Δi,j(k)=∑t(Ξ−1​r)t​n~i​j​kt.\Delta^{(k)}_{i,j}=\sum_{t}(\Xi^{-1}r)_{t}\tilde{n}_{ijk}^{t}. (58)

The proof follows the same arguments as the proof of Lemmas 2 and 7.

Note that to establish a certified bound in the case of 𝒫⁡(G~0(k))⋡0\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}^{(k)})\nsucceq 0 , one cannot simply apply Lemma 5 and lift the Gram blocks independently as in the sparse case, as they are not indexed by the monomial basis in which constraints {ci}\{c_{i}\} are expressed. Instead, one has to lift the full block-diagonal ambient Gram matrix 𝒫(G~0):=diag(𝒫(G~0(1)),..,𝒫(G~0(K)))\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}):=\mathrm{diag}\left(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}^{(1)}),..,\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}^{(K)}_{0})\right), where eigenvalue computations can still be performed block-wise due to the unitary invariance of the matrices’ spectra.

Theorem 10 (Certified bounds in symmetry-adapted bases).

Assume an inaccurate numerical certificate (λd,{G0(k)}k=1K,{Gi(k)}i=1mG)(\lambda_{d},\{G_{0}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K},\{G_{i}^{(k)}\}_{i=1}^{m_{G}}) to an NPO where G0(k)G_{0}^{(k)} are blocks indexed by polynomials {bi(k)}i=1N\{b_{i}^{(k)}\}_{i=1}^{N} that stem from block-diagonalization of a Gram matrix in the monomial basis, and assume variables are subject to one of the constraint sets {ci}\{c_{i}\} from Theorem 4. Let

𝒫⁡(G~0(k))=G~0(k)+Δ(k)k∈[K]\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}^{(k)})=\tilde{G}_{0}^{(k)}+\Delta^{(k)}\quad k\in[K] (59)

be the set of blocks after rounding and projecting according to Lemma 9 with certified bounds to minimal eigenvalues μmink\mu_{\mathrm{min}}^{k}. Then,

λdrat=λ~d+δd=λ~d−mink⁡({μmink,0})⋅sn,dℐ\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{rat}}=\tilde{\lambda}_{d}+\delta_{d}=\tilde{\lambda}_{d}-\min_{k}(\{\mu_{\mathrm{min}}^{k},0\})\cdot s_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}} (60)

constitutes a certified upper bound to the maximization problem, i.e., λdrat≥λmax\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{rat}}\geq\lambda_{\max}.

The proof follows from the invariance of the eigenspectrum under unitary transformations and applying Lemma 5 to 𝒫⁡(G~0)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}) in the monomial basis. Again, if all blocks fulfill 𝒫⁡(G~0(k))≻0\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}^{(k)})\succ 0, the same argument as in Theorem 6 holds, which lets one further tighten the numerical symmetry-adapted bound.

One has to note here that even though the projection scheme in the sparse and symmetric case exhibit a similar structure, they also strongly differ in terms of computational complexity. In the sparse (and trivially, dense) case, one can show that the rationalization scheme carries less computational complexity with respect to the matrix sizes than solving the underlying SDP. However, in the symmetry-adapted case, computing the Frobenius optimal projection may exceed the cost of SDP solving, depending on the block partitioning of the initial Gram matrix G0G_{0}. A discussion of the complexity in both sparsity and symmetry-adapted cases is given in Appendix C.

As a second remark we note that in the case of sparse cliques with sufficiently small overlap, one finds

sn,dℐ>∑ksnCk,dℐs^{\mathcal{I}}_{n,d}>\sum_{k}s_{n_{C_{k}},d}^{\mathcal{I}} (61)

in which case the loss in bounds through rationalization in the dense case, δd\delta_{d}, often exceeds the sparse loss, δdsp\delta_{d}^{\mathrm{sp}}. This fact can lead to the counterintuitive phenomenon that rationalized sparse bounds become tighter than the corresponding rationalized dense bounds, λdsp,rat<λdrat\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{sp,rat}}<\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{rat}}, as it is illustrated in the next section.

5 Maximal quantum violation of Bell inequalities

As a first benchmark for our certification method, as well to demonstrate its necessity, we apply it to the problem of determining the maximal quantum violation of Bell inequalities. All of the numerical experiments in this work were modeled in Julia using the libraries NCTSSOS [54] and QMBCertify [55], and the resulting SDPs were solved with the commercial solver MOSEK [40], using 10−810^{-8} tolerances for primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and the relative duality gap. The solver choice is critical for numerical reliability, where MOSEK was selected for its state-of-the-art interior-point implementation and its widespread adoption in semidefinite optimization. Certified bounds on minimal eigenvalues μmin\mu_{\min} of the rounded and projected Gram matrices (as explained in Section 3.2) have been computed using Arblib.jl [25], where exact rational representations of the certified enclosures returned by Arblib are used for subsequent exact arithmetic operations necessary for the algebraic lifting. The code to obtain certified bounds and reproduce our results is integrated in the Julia libraries NCTSSOS11 1 https://github.com/wangjie212/NCTSSOS/tree/master/examples and QMBCertify22 2 https://github.com/wangjie212/QMBCertify/tree/main/examples packages for Bell and many-body benchmarks respectively.

As an illustrative example, consider the famous Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) inequality [16] ⟨A0​B0⟩+⟨A0​B1⟩+⟨A1​B0⟩−⟨A1​B1⟩≤2.\langle A_{0}B_{0}\rangle+\langle A_{0}B_{1}\rangle+\langle A_{1}B_{0}\rangle-\langle A_{1}B_{1}\rangle\leq 2. Here, ⟨Ai​Bj⟩\langle A_{i}B_{j}\rangle denote expectation values of products of dichotomic observables AiA_{i} and BjB_{j}. Intuitively one can think of a game involving two parties, Alice and Bob, that perform either of the two measurements randomly, trying to maximize the correlations constituting the inequality. Such inequalities characterize the boundaries between local behaviors, admitting a description in terms of local hidden variables, and quantum behaviors, e.g., correlations achievable by measurements on a joint bipartite quantum system. If a given strategy exceeds the local bound, equal to 2 in the case of the CHSH inequality, one can conclude that no local hidden-variable model can reproduce the corresponding correlations, and hence that nonlocal (quantum or supraquantum) resources were used. A central question along these lines is how different the emergent correlations can be for quantum states with respect to local strategies, which is captured in the maximal quantum violation of a given Bell expression, known to be equal to 2​22\sqrt{2} in the CHSH case.

Finding maximal violations of Bell expressions to bound the set of quantum correlations constitutes the first family of problems for which non-commutative SDP relaxations were exploited [42]. Such scenarios can be extended to feature an arbitrary number of parties, measurements per parties, and outcomes per measurement, depending on the setting of interest. In this section we focus on two-party Bell expressions featuring mAm_{A} and mBm_{B} dichotomic measurements on Alice’s and Bob’s side, respectively. In general, an optimization problem of this class reads

λmax\displaystyle\lambda_{\max} =supℋ,|ψ⟩∈ℋ,Ai,Bj∈ℬ⁡(ℋ)∑i=1mA∑j=1mBci​j⟨AiBj⟩\displaystyle=\sup_{\mathcal{H},\ket{\psi}\in\mathcal{H},A_{i},B_{j}\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})}\quad\sum_{i=1}^{m_{A}}\sum_{j=1}^{m_{B}}c_{ij}\langle A_{i}B_{j}\rangle
+∑i=1mAai⟨Ai⟩+∑j=1mBbj⟨Bj⟩\displaystyle+\sum_{i=1}^{m_{A}}a_{i}\langle A_{i}\rangle+\sum_{j=1}^{m_{B}}b_{j}\langle B_{j}\rangle (62)
s.t.Ai2=1,i=1,…,mA,\displaystyle\qquad\mathrm{s.t.}\qquad\quad\quad\,\,A_{i}^{2}=1,\qquad i=1,...,m_{A},
Bj2=1,j=1,…,mB,\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\,\,\,\,B_{j}^{2}=1,\qquad j=1,...,m_{B},
[Ai,Bj]=0,\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\,\,\,\,[A_{i},B_{j}]=0,

where the coefficients {ci​j,ai,bj}\{c_{ij},a_{i},b_{j}\} encrypt the type of Bell inequality, and commutation of AiA_{i} and BjB_{j} is enforced to model the bipartite Hilbert space structure. This problem exhibits the same structure as (2), allowing us to make use of the NPA hierarchy and our certification scheme.

The need for certification already becomes clear in the simplest case of the CHSH inequality: Running hierarchy level d=2d=2 for CHSH yields the following (wrong) upper bound:

λ2≈2.828427122879≱2​2=λmax,\lambda_{2}\,\approx 2.828427122879\ngeq 2\sqrt{2}=\lambda_{\max}, (63)

smaller than the known maximal quantum violation. However, the certified bound fulfills λ2rat>λmax\lambda_{2}^{\mathrm{rat}}>\lambda_{\max}, as illustrated by the following truncated decimal expansion of the exact rational representation:

λ2rat≈ 2.828427125402>2​2=λmax.\lambda_{2}^{\mathrm{rat}}\,\approx\,2.828427125402>2\sqrt{2}=\lambda_{\max}. (64)

We emphasize here that while the numerical bound λ2\lambda_{2} does hold when truncated at the 88th digit, corresponding to the SDP tolerance of the solver, the main conceptual point of this work is to actually certify the soundness of a given bound via an exact algebraic certificate, as it cannot be guaranteed by merely truncating numerical bounds at the expected numerical precision.

5.1 Certified bounds to maximum quantum violations of Bell inequalities A2−A89A_{2}-A_{89}

To further investigate this behavior, we ran our certification methods on a catalog of 88 inequivalent two-party, dichotomic Bell inequalities, called A2−A89A_{2}-A_{89}, first introduced in [24], for relaxation orders d∈{1,2,3}d\in\{1,2,3\}. These problems constitute adequate benchmark problems for our method as accurate numerical reference values have been established for 79/8879/88 inequalities in the benchmarking set [23], allowing us to judge the quality of both the numerical bounds as well as their certified counterparts. Besides this, the catalog carries a manifold of different scenarios and hence Gram matrix sizes, allowing us to test our method on a wide spread of settings. We start with the analysis of the dense certification scheme.

As a first question it is interesting to see how the certification loss

δd:=λdrat−λd=−min{μmin,0}⋅sn,dℐ\delta_{d}:=\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{rat}}-\lambda_{d}=-\min\{\mu_{\min},0\}\cdot s_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}} (65)

is correlated with the quality of the initial numerical certificate: we expect the loss in tightness to be worse if the initial numerical certificate had a large numerical error. To do so, as a measure of inaccuracy of the numerical certificate at relaxation order dd, we introduce the 1-norm 𝒟d\mathcal{D}_{d} of the difference between the numerical left hand side LdL_{d}

Ld=λd​1−f,L_{d}=\lambda_{d}{1}-f, (66)

and the numerical right hand side RdR_{d} of the certificate

Rd=vd∗​G0​vd,R_{d}=v_{d}^{*}G_{0}v_{d}, (67)

in terms of reduced basis words indexed by tt:

𝒟d:=∑t|Ld−Rd|t,\mathcal{D}_{d}:=\sum_{t}|L_{d}-R_{d}|_{t}, (68)

which lets one investigate how the certification loss δd\delta_{d} depends on the inaccuracy of the numerical certificate.

Figure 3(a) shows the behavior of the bound loss δd\delta_{d} depending on the numerical certificate error 𝒟d\mathcal{D}_{d}. One can see empirically that large certificate errors 𝒟d\mathcal{D}_{d} lead to higher bound losses, which is what we intuitively expect: as established in Section 3, the bound loss depends on two variables, the Gram matrix size sn,dℐs_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}}, and the minimal eigenvalue of the projected matrix μmin\mu_{\min} , which are both correlated with the certificate error 𝒟d\mathcal{D}_{d}. We expect both μmin\mu_{\min} and sn,dℐs_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}} to independently affect the bound loss δd\delta_{d}, which is further examined in the following figures.

Figure 3(b) shows the trend that larger numerical certificate errors produce larger distances of projected matrices 𝒫⁡(G~0)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}) to the PSD cone. This is expected, as large certificate errors lead to large Frobenius distances between 𝒫⁡(G~0)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}) and G0G_{0}, possibly projecting the matrices further out of the PSD cone to achieve coefficient equalities. Hence, we expect the minimal, negative, projected eigenvalue bound μmin\mu_{\min} to grow in magnitude as the numerical certificate error 𝒟d\mathcal{D}_{d} worsens, yielding larger certification losses δd\delta_{d}.

Figure 3(c) shows the behavior of the bound loss δd\delta_{d} with respect to the Gram matrix size sn,dℐs_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}}. As the two are multiplicatively correlated, we see that larger sn,dℐs_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}} can result in larger δd\delta_{d}. However, one can also see that at a fixed size sn,dℐs_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}}, the bound loss has a high variance, which is reflected by the variance in certificate errors 𝒟d\mathcal{D}_{d} and hence minimal eigenvalues μmin\mu_{\min}. This indicates that the quality of the numerical certificate is at least as important as the combinatorial growth for the tightness of the certified bounds.

To summarize, our first benchmarks indicate that a large numerical certificate error 𝒟d\mathcal{D}_{d} often leads to a large bound loss δd\delta_{d}, firstly due to the correlation of 𝒟d\mathcal{D}_{d} and δd\delta_{d} with the size sn,dℐs_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}} of the Gram matrix, and secondly through the larger Frobenius distance ‖𝒫⁡(G~0)−G~0‖F\|\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})-\tilde{G}_{0}\|_{F} induced through projection, enabling larger negative eigenvalues μmin\mu_{\min}.

In [23], the authors established that relaxations for the majority of Bell inequalities A2−A89A_{2}-A_{89} match constructive lower bounds up to the numerical accuracy of 10−810^{-8} at latest at order d=3d=3, where the obtained reference maximal violations λref\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}} are computed in [46, 47]. Splitting the inequalities into three sets, ℬi,i∈{1,2,3}\mathcal{B}_{i},i\in\{1,2,3\} according to the hierarchy level at which the lower and upper bounds numerically coincide (sorting the remaining inequalities to ℬ3\mathcal{B}_{3}), allows us to investigate the behavior of the obtained numerical bounds, as well as the certified bounds, with respect to these reference maximal violations. As |ℬ1|=2|\mathcal{B}_{1}|=2, we restrict the analysis to the cases of ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} and ℬ3\mathcal{B}_{3}.

Figure 4 shows how the numerical and rational bounds relate to the numerical reference maximal violations33 3 Bell inequalities with indices i∈{7,9,10,15,28,42,44,48,66}i\in\{7,9,10,15,28,42,44,48,66\} are not displayed because their numerical bounds hold by a significant margin.. Note that a point in the positive halfspace denotes a bound which is consistent with the reference values, while points in the negative halfspace are necessarily invalid. We see that while a significant fraction of the numerical bounds λd\lambda_{d} at both relaxation orders are invalid, all produced rational bounds are proper upper bounds to λref\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}. In fact, we find that 6/20 numerical bounds in ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} are incorrect, while 26/66 bounds in ℬ3\mathcal{B}_{3} are incorrect. This demonstration highlights the necessity of certified bounds as reliable alternatives to their numerical counterparts.

5.2 Comparison between the dense and sparse scheme

While the minimal projected eigenvalue μmin\mu_{\min} inherently depends on the certificate error 𝒟d\mathcal{D}_{d}, and hence on the numerical precision of the solver, one can mitigate the dependence on the Gram matrix size by making use of the sparse hierarchy and associated certification scheme. To do so, we applied the sparse scheme to the same set of Bell inequalities and compared the sparse certification bound loss δdsp\delta_{d}^{\mathrm{sp}} to the dense one.

Figure 5 shows the difference between the dense and the sparse bound loss, δd−δdsp\delta_{d}-\delta_{d}^{\mathrm{sp}} for different relaxation orders d∈{1,2,3}d\in\{1,2,3\}. Points in the positive half space hence correspond to experiments where δd>δdsp\delta_{d}>\delta_{d}^{\mathrm{sp}}, i.e., where the sparse certification scheme lead to a smaller bound correction after projection.

As one can see, often times the dense loss δd\delta_{d} exceeds the sparse loss δdsp\delta_{d}^{\mathrm{sp}}, which, when neglecting the distribution of minimal eigenvalues, can be explained by the often smaller total problem size in the sparse case with respect to the dense case. As discussed in Section 4, by exploiting sparsity, some monomials, i.e., those involving variables from different cliques, do not appear in any of the sparse gram matrices, while they do in the dense description. On the other hand, a large variable overlap of cliques could cause the sum of sparse block sizes (∑ksnk,dℐ\sum_{k}s_{n_{k},d}^{\mathcal{I}}) to become larger than the dense block size (sn,dℐs_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}}). However, if the overlap is small enough, the total size will be smaller than in the dense case, which is reflected in the figures.

This behavior can lead to the counterintuitive phenomenon that the certified sparse bounds become tighter than their rational dense counterparts, in stark contrast to results from the numerical relaxations. This happens exactly when the excess in δd\delta_{d} compensates for the numerical difference λd<λdsp\lambda_{d}<\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{sp}}. In our experiments we find that at d=1d=1, 70/89 rational sparse bounds were tighter than the dense counterparts. At d=3d=3 we find that 6/88 sparse bounds were tighter, while at d=2d=2 all dense bounds were tighter. This dependency on the relaxation order can be explained by two competing mechanisms, assuming cliques with sufficiently small overlap: On the one hand, the numerical bound difference λd−λdsp\lambda_{d}-\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{sp}} is expected to increase with increasing dd, as the sparse hierarchy fails to capture the increasing amount of clique overlap monomials. On the other hand, the dense Gram matrix size grows more rapidly with dd, leading to a larger multiplicative factor when computing the certified bounds λdrat\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{rat}}.

5.3 Tilted CHSH inequality

As a last benchmark in the non-locality scenario we investigated the performance of our scheme to estimate the maximal quantum violation of a variant of the so called tilted CHSH inequality [1], introduced in [21]:

ℬt​(θA,θB)\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{t}(\theta_{A},\theta_{B}) =∑x,y(−1)x​y​⟨Ax​By⟩+θA​⟨A0⟩+θB​⟨B0⟩\displaystyle=\sum_{x,y}(-1)^{xy}\langle A_{x}B_{y}\rangle+\theta_{A}\langle A_{0}\rangle+\theta_{B}\langle B_{0}\rangle
≤2+θA+θB.\displaystyle\leq 2+\theta_{A}+\theta_{B}. (69)

The study of said inequality poses a computationally relevant problem for our framework: On the one hand, this tilted CHSH inequality is self-testing, and the authors provide an analytical solution for its maximal quantum violation. On the other hand, the authors show that this tilted CHSH inequality is intractable using the NPA hierarchy as θA+θB→2\theta_{A}+\theta_{B}\rightarrow 2, as increasingly high relaxation levels are needed for convergence. In fact, the authors showed, using the arbitrary-precision solver SDPA-GMP [41], that for parameters θA=θB=0.999\theta_{A}=\theta_{B}=0.999, even NPA level d=10d=10 does not achieve the analytical optimal violation. This provides an interesting application for the certification scheme, as it allows us (a) to investigate its performance at high relaxation orders without finite convergence and (b) compare computed bounds to the exact maximum quantum violations.

As one can see in Figure 6, even though high-precision calculations showed that the hierarchy does not converge at the displayed relaxation orders, the numerical upper bounds λd\lambda_{d} computed with MOSEK are below the analytical maximum for relaxation orders d>4d>4, resulting in wrong bounds, which furthermore do not monotonically decrease. On the other hand, our certification scheme produces valid bounds at all relaxation orders, with the tightest bound achieved at order d=7d=7. In this scenario where numerical bounds are stagnating, the certified bounds start to worsen due to the rapid growth of sn,dℐs_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}} with respect to dd.

6 Ground-state observables in quantum many-body systems

A primary objective of quantum many-body physics is to understand the properties of the state of minimal energy, or ground state of a physical system. A conceptually simple method to do so is exact diagonalization, where one represents the Hamiltonian describing a system as a matrix in a chosen basis and computes its full eigenspectrum numerically [56]. While this method provides numerically exact solutions, the Hilbert space dimension typically grows exponentially with the particle number NN (for instance, dimℋ=2N\dim\mathcal{H}=2^{N} for NN spin-1/21/2 particles), rendering exact diagonalization infeasible rapidly. To mitigate this, one often restricts the variational ground-state search to physically motivated manifolds [57]. Notably, tensor network methods [15], e.g. Matrix-Product States or Projected Entangled Pair States, have been shown to significantly scale up the feasible problem sizes. However, a variational Ansatz, in general, does not provide any guarantee for how well the Ansatz space captures the actual ground state of the problem, and can just provide upper bounds to the true ground-state energy

E0v​a​r≥E0.E_{0}^{var}\geq E_{0}. (70)

For any other observable, variational methods just offer an estimation, with no guarantee of how close it is to the true value or whether it bounds it from above or below. The NPA hierarchy constitutes a counterpart to these variational Ansätze by virtue of relaxation, hence allowing one to (numerically) certify an interval for E0E_{0}:

E0v​a​r≥E0≥E0SDP.E_{0}^{var}\geq E_{0}\geq E_{0}^{\mathrm{SDP}}. (71)

Now, in [55] the authors make use of such inequality constraints on the ground-state energy to obtain bounds on ground-state observables beyond the energy (e.g. magnetization and local correlators). This constitutes a particularly interesting application for our method, as it constitutes one of the aforementioned iterative algorithms, reusing SDP bounds of former runs in consecutive programs. If wrong numerical lower bounds are issued, E0SDP≰E0E_{0}^{\mathrm{SDP}}\nleq E_{0}, imposing such a wrong inequality in the computation of other ground state observables might cause an accumulation of errors. Our certification method precisely eliminates this failure mode by turning the SDP output into a rigorously valid lower bound.

We start by applying our certification scheme to the computation of ground state energies of the translationally invariant J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} Heisenberg chain with nearest- and second-nearest neighbor interactions and periodic boundary conditions with Hamiltonian

H=14​∑i=1N∑a∈{x,y,z}(σia​σi+1a+J2​σia​σi+2a),H=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{a\in\{x,y,z\}}\left(\sigma_{i}^{a}\,\sigma_{i+1}^{a}+J_{2}\,\sigma_{i}^{a}\,\sigma_{i+2}^{a}\right), (72)

where σia\sigma_{i}^{a} denotes the Pauli operator of type aa acting on site ii. We adapt the convention J1=1J_{1}=1 from the underlying work.

In [55, 53], the authors exploit sparsity and various symmetries to significantly improve the scalability of the hierarchy, allowing them to study large system sizes. Exploiting the sign symmetry of the model lets one block-diagonalize the dense Gram matrix into four smaller blocks G(j),j∈{1,2,3,4}G^{(j)},j\in\{1,2,3,4\}. Due to the model’s symmetry under permutation of the Pauli operators {σix,σiy,σiz}\{\sigma_{i}^{x},\sigma_{i}^{y},\sigma_{i}^{z}\} , one can identify three of the blocks with each other, leaving one with two independent PSD blocks G(j),j∈{1,2}G^{(j)},j\in\{1,2\} which can be further block diagonalized to blocks Gi(j),i∈{1,…,N/2+1}G_{i}^{(j)},i\in\{1,\ldots,N/2+1\} due to the translational symmetry of the model. The associated transformation is the discrete Fourier transform P∈ℂN×NP\in\mathbb{C}^{N\times N}:

Pi,j=1Ne−2π𝐢(i−1)(j−1)/N,i,j=1,…,N.P_{i,j}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\mathrm{e}^{-2\pi\mathbf{i}(i-1)(j-1)/N},\quad i,j=1,\ldots,N. (73)

For details on these symmetry exploitations the reader is directed to [53].

After exploiting the symmetries, the numerical SOHS certificate for lower bounds λd\lambda_{d} to said ground state problems can be obtained as

Figure 7 shows the results for applying our certification scheme to a J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} Heisenberg chain up to length N=50N=50. One can see from Figure 7(a) that the certified bounds are consistent with the upper bounds computed by DMRG, recovering the results from [55]. Figure 7(b) shows the bound shift by going from numerical to rational bounds depending on NN. What is remarkable here is that in this scenario the bound shift decreases with an increasing problem size. In conclusion, this first experiment suggests that the numerical results of the certification method seem to improve when symmetries are exploited. However, they also come with an increased computational cost, as it is shown in Appendix C.

To obtain a rational certificate from the numerical one, one first has to establish rational, certified bounds on E0E_{0} for the multiplier terms. For the SDP bound we use the previously established certified lower bounds on HH. As establishing certified variational bounds is not the scope of this work, we use E0v​a​r,r​a​t=(E0v​a​r+δ​E0)~E_{0}^{var,rat}=\widetilde{(E_{0}^{var}+\delta E_{0})} as a rational upper bound, where δ​E0\delta E_{0} is chosen larger than the DMRG precision, and the rounding precision η\eta of lower magnitude than δ​E0\delta E_{0} to ensure a valid bound. We start by investigating nearest-neighbor correlations ⟨σia​σi+1a⟩\langle\sigma^{a}_{i}\sigma^{a}_{i+1}\rangle in the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} Heisenberg chain of length N=12N=12 dependent on the second-nearest neighbor couplings J2J_{2}. The results are shown in Figure 8, where we are able to certify antiferromagnetic correlations ⟨σia​σi+1a⟩<0\langle\sigma^{a}_{i}\sigma^{a}_{i+1}\rangle<0 for all J2J_{2}, recovering the results from [55]. Figure 9 shows the corresponding bound shifts δd\delta_{d}, where we find no obvious correlations between the shifts δd\delta_{d} and the coupling J2J_{2}. As the problem size sn,dℐs_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}} is fixed for all J2J_{2}, the differences in δd\delta_{d} stem solely from differences in minimal eigenvalues μmini​j\mu^{ij}_{\min} of the projected Gram blocks. This indicates that the numerical problem is equally well conditioned for all J2J_{2}, in stark contrast to the following application.

Figure 10 shows certified bounds to second neighbor spin correlations ⟨σia​σi+2a⟩\langle\sigma_{i}^{a}\sigma_{i+2}^{a}\rangle in the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} Heisenberg chain of length N=12N=12. We are able to certify ferromagnetic correlations ⟨σia​σi+2a⟩>0\langle\sigma_{i}^{a}\sigma_{i+2}^{a}\rangle>0 for couplings J2≤J2+<0.5J_{2}\leq J^{+}_{2}<0.5, and antiferromagnetic correlations ⟨σia​σi+2a⟩<0\langle\sigma_{i}^{a}\sigma_{i+2}^{a}\rangle<0 for J2≥J2−>0.5J_{2}\geq J^{-}_{2}>0.5. Note that in the analysis of [55], the transition point was exactly at J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5. At this value, the so called Majumdar-Ghosh point, two exactly degenerate ground states |ψ1⟩\ket{\psi_1} and |ψ2⟩\ket{\psi_2} emerge [39], leading to a distinct behavior in the observed bound shift, as displayed in Figure 11: Remarkably, while for J2≠0.5J_{2}\neq 0.5 projected Gram matrices 𝒫⁡(G~i(j))\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{i}^{(j)}) with negative minimal eigenvalues μmini​j<0\mu^{ij}_{\min}<0 emerge, for J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5 the numerical, as well as the projected Gram blocks, lie on the interior of the PSD cone, carrying positive minimal eigenvalues μmini​j>0\mu^{ij}_{\min}>0 of relatively large magnitude. This is in accordance with the observation of the SDP solver not being able to provide an optimal solution at J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5, but issuing a feasible point: As the objective function is linear and the feasible set is the intersection of an affine space ℒ\mathcal{L} and the PSD cone, optimal numerical solutions have to lie on the boundary of the PSD cone and approximately fulfill μmini​j≈0\mu^{ij}_{\min}\approx 0. In the case of μmini​j>0\mu^{ij}_{\min}>0, we are able to tighten the bounds to our problem by applying Theorem 6 (i) to shift the projected blocks from the interior of the PSD cone to its boundary.

This apparent ill-conditioning can be explained by the two-fold degeneracy of the ground state at J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5: As |ψ1⟩\ket{\psi_1} and |ψ2⟩\ket{\psi_2} share exactly the same ground state energy E0E_{0}, any convex combination will do so too, leading to an increase in dimensionality of the optimal subspace. Hence, the energy constraints employed to compute bounds on ⟨σia​σi+2a⟩\langle\sigma_{i}^{a}\sigma_{i+2}^{a}\rangle do not restrict the search space in the same manner as for problems with non-degenerate ground states, as it is the case for the other investigated values of J2J_{2} for a finite chain.

This phenomenon suggests that, while in general our certification procedure produces weakened bounds, it is possible to construct tighter rational bounds λdrat\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{rat}} with respect to their numerical counterpart λd\lambda_{d} if SDP solutions are issued in the interior of the PSD cone. Conclusively, this suggests a second possible application of our method to obtain certified and tighter bounds to problems which are intractable to SDP solvers.

7 Conclusion and Outlook

In this work we presented a constructive method to obtain certified outer bounds to non-commutative optimization problems by postprocessing numerical data obtained from the NPA hierarchy. We do so by extracting an exact SOHS certificate from an SDP solver’s Gram data, which consists of (1) rounding the data to rationals (2) performing a Frobenius optimal projection back onto the affine constraint subspace, and (3) a constraint dependent lifting of the projected Gram matrices into the PSD cone. We further extended this procedure to sparsity and symmetry-adapted scenarios, and analyzed the method’s complexity relative to the underlying SDP. We also provided a tightening procedure which for PD projected Gram matrices leads to tighter, certified bounds.

We then applied our method to obtain certified bounds on (a) the maximal violation of a catalog of bipartite Bell inequalities, and (b) quantum many-body ground-state observables, where we found moderate losses in tightness that reflect a justified cost for obtaining rigorous guarantees. In the sparse case we observed that sparse rational bounds can become tighter than their dense counterparts, while in the symmetry-adapted scenario we identified a computational bottleneck that we suspect to be common to any SDP-based computer-assisted proof in arbitrary symmetry-adapted bases. In addition, we also find that in regimes of inexact SDP termination, the rational bounds can become tighter than their numerical, uncertified counterparts, which is of independent interest when dealing with numerical instabilities. In summary, we provided analytical constructions and numerical evidence that promote numerical semidefinite relaxations toward computer-assisted proofs in quantum theory.

Our method is readily extendable to modified non-commutative hierarchies such as trace- or state-optimization, as they differ from the presented hierarchy solely up to moment equality constraints. Following the same argument, it is also possible to extend this method to differentially constrained non-commutative polynomial optimization problems, allowing one to certify non-polynomial quantities in quantum theory. We also emphasize that if our post-processing framework proves applicable to non-commutative optimization problems arising in other application domains, this would further enhance its significance.

There are two main venues for further investigation, namely (i) optimality of the bound-lifting step in the dense case, and (ii) scalability in the symmetry-adapted setting: Since our bound-lifting strategy scales with the size of the Gram blocks, which grows rapidly in the dense hierarchy, we observe increasing bound losses at higher relaxation orders. A refined bound-lifting procedure featuring a more involved spectral analysis of the Gram matrices, or a proof of optimality of the presented method hence deserve further investigation. Secondly, as we showed in Appendix C, when Gram blocks are indexed by polynomial bases, even establishing the numerical non-negativity certificate might exceed the cost of solving the associated SDP. Understanding how structure exploitation of the unitary basis change might reduce the certificate complexity is hence another open question. In addition, it would be interesting to systematically quantify the dependence of the certification loss on solver accuracy: Using higher-precision solvers should yield more accurate numerical certificates and hence smaller bound differences δd\delta_{d}, at the expense of computational efficiency. Regarding the last point, it would be also interesting to obtain lower bounds on the relaxed maxima, providing the counterpart to our certified bounds and yielding certified enclosures for the initial numerical upper bound, allowing one to further judge its quality, e.g., as demonstrated in [8]. To do so, one has to apply the projection on the dual (pseudo-moment) side of the certificate, where the exact projection onto the pseudo-moment cone poses the main technical challenge.

Beyond these directions, it would also be worthwhile to further study the certification scheme for numerically delicate instances in which the solver returns solutions strictly inside the PSD cone, and to systematically leverage such cases to obtain tighter bounds.

Appendix A Proof of Lemma 5

We deal with the four different constraint families separately.
Box and unipotency constraints. Assume {ci}i=1,..,n={1−Xi2}i=1,..,n⊆G\{c_{i}\}_{i=1,..,n}=\{1-X_{i}^{2}\}_{i=1,..,n}\subseteq G, e.g. Box constraints. We show that for ε>0\varepsilon>0 there exists the following rational decomposition

ε​sn,d=ε​vd∗​vd+∑i,kqk​i∗​(1−Xi2)​qk​i.\varepsilon s_{n,d}=\varepsilon v_{d}^{*}v_{d}+\sum_{i,k}q_{ki}^{\ast}(1-X_{i}^{2})q_{ki}. (77)

with polynomials qk​i∈ℚd−1​⟨X¯⟩q_{ki}\in\mathbb{Q}_{d-1}\langle\underline{X}\rangle. To do so, we first show that

1=w∗​w+∑i,kqk​i∗​(1−Xi2)​qk​i.1=w^{*}w\;+\;\sum_{i,k}q_{ki}^{*}(1-X_{i}^{2})q_{ki}. (78)

for all monomials ww with |w|≤d|w|\leq d. Proceed by induction on dd. The variables XjX_{j} yield the base case for words of length |w|=1|w|=1:

1=Xj2+(1−Xj2).1=X_{j}^{2}+(1-X_{j}^{2}). (79)

Assume the induction hypothesis (78) holds for ww with |w|≤d−1|w|\leq d-1. Multiplying by XjX_{j} from both sides gives

Xj2=u∗​u+∑i,kXj​qk​i∗​(1−Xi2)​qk​i​Xj.X_{j}^{2}=u^{*}u+\sum_{i,k}X_{j}q_{ki}^{*}(1-X_{i}^{2})q_{ki}X_{j}. (80)

with u=Xj​wu=X_{j}w. Plugging this expression into (79) yields

1=u∗​u+∑i,kXj​qk​i∗​(1−Xi2)​qk​i​Xj+(1−Xj2)1=u^{*}u+\sum_{i,k}X_{j}q_{ki}^{\ast}(1-X_{i}^{2})q_{ki}X_{j}+(1-X_{j}^{2})

which is of the desired form. Summing over all uu with |u|≤d|u|\leq d and multiplying by ε\varepsilon proves the claim (77). The full argument also holds for unipotency constraints.

Ball constraints. Assume c1=(1−∑iXi2)∈Gc_{1}=(1-\sum_{i}X_{i}^{2})\in G. We want to show the existence of

ε​sn,d​1=ε​vd∗​vd+∑krk∗​rk+∑kqk∗​(1−∑iXi2)​qk.\varepsilon s_{n,d}{1}=\varepsilon v_{d}^{*}v_{d}+\sum_{k}r_{k}^{\ast}r_{k}+\sum_{k}q_{k}^{\ast}\Bigl(1-\sum_{i}X_{i}^{2}\Bigr)q_{k}. (81)

for ε>0\varepsilon>0, rk∈ℚd​⟨X¯⟩r_{k}\in\mathbb{Q}_{d}\langle\underline{X}\rangle and qk∈ℚd−1​⟨X¯⟩q_{k}\in\mathbb{Q}_{d-1}\langle\underline{X}\rangle. We again proceed by induction on |w||w|, where we want to show that for all ww with |w|≤d|w|\leq d

+(Xj−1)2+ 2​(Xj−Xj2)\displaystyle\quad+(X_{j}-1)^{2}\;+\;2(X_{j}-X_{j}^{2}) (90)

which is of the target SOHS form, yielding (86) by summing over all words and multiplying by ε\varepsilon. We note that the same argument also holds for {ci}i=1n⊆G\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\subseteq G.

Appendix B Proof of Theorem 6

Proof of Theorem 6.

We start by proving the tightening scheme (i) from the Theorem.

Let (λ~d,𝒫⁡(G~0))\left(\tilde{\lambda}_{d},\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})\right) be an exact pre-certificate obtained after rounding and projection

λ~d​1−f=vd∗​𝒫​(G~0)​vdmod​ℐ,\tilde{\lambda}_{d}{1}-f\;=\;v_{d}^{*}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})\,v_{d}\qquad\mathrm{mod}\,\mathcal{I}, (91)

and let 𝒫⁡(G~0)≻0\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})\succ 0 admit a positive lower bound μmin>0\mu_{\min}>0 to its eigenspectrum. Recall the following constant SOHS decomposition from Equation 77 in Appendix A:

sn,d​1=vd∗​vd+∑i,kqk​i∗​(1−Xi2)​qk​is_{n,d}{1}=v_{d}^{*}v_{d}+\sum_{i,k}q_{ki}^{*}(1-X_{i}^{2})q_{ki} (92)

Multiplying by any ε∈ℝ\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R} and working modulo the underlying ideal then yields the following relation

ε​sn,dℐ​1=ε​vd∗​vdmodℐ\varepsilon s_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}}{1}=\varepsilon v_{d}^{*}v_{d}\mod\mathcal{I} (93)

where this holds particularly for ε<0\varepsilon<0 and hence for ε=−μmin<0\varepsilon=-\mu_{\min}<0. This relation follows from the vector space property of the ideal. Adding Equations 91 and 93 then yields the following certificate in the quotient space

(λ~d​1−μmin​sn,dℐ)−f=\displaystyle\left(\tilde{\lambda}_{d}{1}-\mu_{\min}s_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}}\right)-f\;= (94)
vd∗​(𝒫⁡(G~0)−μmin​1)​vdmod​ℐ,\displaystyle v_{d}^{*}\left(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})\,-\mu_{\min}{1}\right)v_{d}\quad\mathrm{mod}\,\mathcal{I},

which certifies λdrat=(λ~d−μmin​sn,dℐ)<λ~d\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{rat}}=\left(\tilde{\lambda}_{d}-\mu_{\min}s_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}}\right)<\tilde{\lambda}_{d} as an upper bound to the optimization problem.

We will now prove the second tightening scheme (ii) of the Theorem. Again, assume an exact precertificate as in Equation 91, where no further assumptions on the constraints of the problem are taken. Our goal is to find the maximum τ>0\tau>0 such that the following rank-1 downdate is still PSD:

𝒫⁡(G~0)−τ​e0​e0∗⪰0\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})\,-\tau e_{0}e_{0}^{*}\succeq 0 (95)

considering such downgraded matrix then leads to the following SOHS decomposition

(λ~d−τ)​1−f=vd∗​(𝒫⁡(G~0)−τ​e0​e0∗)​vd​mod​ℐ,.\small\left(\tilde{\lambda}_{d}-\tau\right){1}-f=v_{d}^{*}\left(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})\,-\tau e_{0}e_{0}^{*}\right)v_{d}\hskip 9.24994pt\mathrm{mod}\,\mathcal{I},. (96)

Start by considering the following block hermitian matrix

S:=(𝒫⁡(G~0)e0e0∗τ−1)S:=\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})&e_{0}\\ e_{0}^{*}&\tau^{-1}\end{pmatrix} (97)

Now, the Schur complement of τ−1\tau^{-1} lets one characterize the PSD condition 95:

(𝒫⁡(G~0)−τ​e0​e0∗)⪰0⇔S⪰0\left(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})-\tau e_{0}e_{0}^{*}\right)\succeq 0\Leftrightarrow S\succeq 0 (98)

On the other hand, the Schur complement of 𝒫⁡(G~0)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}) yields

τ−1−e0∗​𝒫​(G~0)−1​e0≥0⇔S⪰0.\tau^{-1}-e_{0}^{*}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})^{-1}e_{0}\geq 0\Leftrightarrow S\succeq 0. (99)

Putting both arguments together yields

(𝒫⁡(G~0)−τ​e0​e0∗)⪰0⇔τ≤1e0∗​𝒫​(G~0)−1​e0\left(\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})-\tau e_{0}e_{0}^{*}\right)\succeq 0\Leftrightarrow\tau\leq\frac{1}{e_{0}^{*}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})^{-1}e_{0}} (100)

Hence, for τ=1e0∗​𝒫​(G~0)−1​e0\tau=\frac{1}{e_{0}^{*}\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})^{-1}e_{0}}, Equation 96 is a valid SOHS certificate, certifying λdrat=λ~d−τ\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{rat}}=\tilde{\lambda}_{d}-\tau as a valid upper bound to the optimization problem. One finds τ∈[μmin,μmax]\tau\in[\mu_{\min},\mu_{\max}] due to the relation of the eigenspectra of 𝒫⁡(G~0)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}) and its inverse. We also note that as 𝒫⁡(G~0)∈ℚsn,dℐ×sn,dℐ\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0})\in\mathbb{Q}^{s_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}}\times s_{n,d}^{\mathcal{I}}} we have τ∈ℚ\tau\in\mathbb{Q}, which is why no further rationalization is needed if the exact inverse of 𝒫⁡(G~0)\mathcal{P}(\tilde{G}_{0}) is computed. ∎

Appendix C Complexity considerations

In this section we address the computational complexity of the projection schemes in Lemmas 7 and 9 (dense, sparse, and symmetry-adapted), as well as the complexity to compute the associated bound shift δd\delta_{d}.

First we show that the projection scheme (7), dense or sparse, over a binomial ideal is computationally less complex than solving the underlying SDP. We give the argument in the sparse case as it trivially includes the dense case. We adopt the standard interior-point complexity model, in which an SDP with SS blocks of maximal size NN requires 𝒪⁡(S​N3)\mathcal{O}(SN^{3}) arithmetic operations per iteration, and 𝒪⁡(S​N)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{SN}) iterations [9]. As the scaling with respect to the number of constraints involved is not made explicit, this constitutes an agnostic lower bound on the overall complexity.

According to Theorem 8, the Frobenius optimal projection over a quotient space generated by a binomial ideal is given by

Δα,β(k)=r𝒩⁡(α∗​β)nℐ​(α,β,k)\Delta^{(k)}_{\alpha,\beta}=\frac{r_{\mathcal{N}(\alpha^{*}\beta)}}{n_{\mathcal{I}}(\alpha,\beta,k)} (101)

Now, for SS cliques and associated Gram blocks with largest blocksize NN, this update has asymptotic complexity 𝒪⁡(S​N2)\mathcal{O}(SN^{2}). To compute the maps nℐ​(α,β,k)n_{\mathcal{I}}(\alpha,\beta,k), one has to iterate over all blocks SS of maximal size N2N^{2}, also yielding complexity 𝒪⁡(S​N2)\mathcal{O}(SN^{2}). Now, once the maps nℐ​(α,β,k)n_{\mathcal{I}}(\alpha,\beta,k) are computed, the residuals r𝒩⁡(α∗​β)r_{\mathcal{N}(\alpha^{*}\beta)} are also obtained in 𝒪⁡(S​N2)\mathcal{O}(SN^{2}) according to Equation (46), leading to a total complexity of 𝒪⁡(S​N2)\mathcal{O}(SN^{2}), which is dominated by the SDP cost per iteration of 𝒪⁡(S​N3)\mathcal{O}(SN^{3}).

We are now going to show that in the case of Gram matrices indexed by non-monomial bases, as it is the case when a Gram matrix is block diagonalized due to symmetry, the computational complexity of the rationalization scheme can become dominant depending on the problem parameters.

Assume a given Gram matrix can be block diagonalized due to symmetries of the problem, as it is the case in [55]. Assume that after block-diagonalization we are again left with SS blocks of maximal size NN. Each Gram block kk is indexed by a polynomial basis

bi(k)=∑α∈S​Nbα,i(k)​vαb_{i}^{(k)}=\sum_{\alpha\in SN}b_{\alpha,i}^{(k)}v_{\alpha} (102)

where (vα)α=1S​N(v_{\alpha})_{\alpha=1}^{SN} indexes the Gram matrix G0G_{0}, e.g., constitutes the monomial indexing basis before block diagonalization. The naive projection would be to transform the large block diagonal matrix back to the monomial basis, losing the block diagonal structure and ending up with complexity 𝒪⁡(S2​N2)\mathcal{O}(S^{2}N^{2}) according to the previous dense argument. In that case, the algorithm is quadratic in SS while the SDP solving cost is linear in SS. Thus, in the case of many small blocks, performing the projection in the monomial basis might become more costly than solving the SDP.

Secondly, one can perform the projection directly in the polynomial basis as in Lemma 9. Defining all variables accordingly, the numerical certificate reads

𝒩​(f−λ​1)t≈∑i,j,kn~i​j​kt​Gi​j(k)\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(f-\lambda{1})_{t}\approx\sum_{i,j,k}\tilde{n}_{ijk}^{t}G_{ij}^{(k)} (103)

Now, in case of the underlying ideal ℐ\mathcal{I} being binomial, the map ni​j​ktn_{ijk}^{t} reads

n~i​j​kt=∑α,βS​N(bi,α(k))∗​bj,β(k)​δ𝒩⁡(α∗​β),t\tilde{n}_{ijk}^{t}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}^{SN}(b_{i,\alpha}^{(k)})^{*}b_{j,\beta}^{(k)}\delta_{\mathcal{N}(\alpha^{*}\beta),t} (104)

In the most general case, each indexing polynomial bi(k)b_{i}^{(k)} can have the whole monomial basis of size S​NSN as its support. This leads to a complexity of building n~i​j​kt\tilde{n}_{ijk}^{t} in a polynomial basis of 𝒪⁡(S2​N2)\mathcal{O}(S^{2}N^{2}), which for large SS dominates the linear cost in SS per SDP iteration.

The complexity argument above also holds for the establishment of numerical SOHS certificates involving symmetries from SDP data and is hence independent of our rationalization scheme. This implies that any SOHS-based proof for non-negativity in symmetry-adapted bases might become computationally more complex than solving the underlying SDP, which constitutes a general bottleneck for SDP assisted proofs for non-negativity in symmetry-adapted scenarios.

Note that besides the asymptotic argument, there is an associated cost per arithmetic operation performed in rational numbers. Depending on the rounding accuracy, the rationalized Gram matrix entries will have numerators and denominators of large bit size. Depending on the size of the rational numbers, rational arithmetic can become orders of magnitude more expensive than the associated operations using floating point numbers. This introduces a degree of freedom, where one can trade rounding accuracy and hence quality of the result for computational complexity.

In addition to performing the projection, to obtain a certified bound λdrat\lambda_{d}^{\mathrm{rat}}, one needs to compute the minimal eigenvalues of the projected Gram matrices, where in the sparse case this results in complexity 𝒪⁡(S​N3)\mathcal{O}(SN^{3}), which is dominated by the overall SDP complexity. In the symmetry-adapted scenario, while the projection complexity is independent of the choice of basis, the eigenvalue computation complexity does heavily depend on the choice: Performing the eigenvalue computation in the inflated monomial basis results in a complexity of 𝒪⁡(S3​N3)\mathcal{O}(S^{3}N^{3}) while computing the eigenvalues in the block-diagonal basis has complexity 𝒪⁡(S​N3)\mathcal{O}(SN^{3}). Hence, for large SS the eigenvalue computation in the monomial basis might become more costly than solving the underlying SDP, while the computation in the symmetry-adapted basis is always cheaper. Hence, from a computational point of view, it is preferable to perform the certification scheme in the symmetry-adapted basis than translating back to the monomial basis.

These asymptotic considerations are consistent with our numerical observations: In the Bell example, projection and eigenvalue costs remain negligible relative to the SDP solving, while in the many-body scenario the combination of high rounding precision and a large number of small blocks lead to the projection eventually becoming the bottleneck of the computation.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
